articles.title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
articles.summary: Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role, and will Neuer's future have an indirect…

image.caption: Many believe Jonas Urbig (right) is the natural successor to Manuel Neuer (left)Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: After Germany's early exit from the 2026 World Cup, Manuel Neuer retired from international duty, opening the door for a new number one.

Jonas Urbig appears the obvious choice, but Neuer is still number one at Bayern Munich, which severely limits Urbig's playing time. If the 23-year-old was Bayern's first choice, he would likely be Germany's number one too. As it stands, though, it appears doubtful that Germany's new coach Jürgen Klopp will even call him up to his first squad. On September 17, he will announce his squad for four UEFA Nations League games against the Netherlands, Greece, and Serbia. And no position in the current Germany team is more up for grabs than goalkeeper.
Oliver Baumann: The automatic Neuer replacement?

Oliver Baumann represents exactly that kind of selfless number two that could be the next number one. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper even commendably dealt with the humiliation of being replaced by Neuer just before the World Cup.

blocks.caption: Oliver Baumann appears unlikely to be Germany's new number one under KloppImage: Michael Memmler/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Klopp isn’t just tasked with celebrating short-term success with Germany. His remit is to bring about lasting change, making Germany favorites for a World Cup and a Euros once again. Oliver Baumann turned 36 this summer. The Bundesliga veteran will be 38 at the next Euros, 40 by the 2030 World Cup. His age might count against a sustainable rebirth of the Germany team.

The Hoffenheim goalkeeper, who has 13 caps, spoke to Bild in the days leading up to the squad announcement about his exchange with Klopp: "Yes, I was in contact with him. He'll say everything else on Thursday. We'll see about the rest—that’s for him to handle."
Ter Stegen: Back in Germany colors via Ajax?

Since Klopp prefers a highly attacking style of play in which all players press high up the field, he might opt for a goalkeeper who can also take on the duties of a field player. Marc-André ter Stegen would fit this profile better than Baumann. Ter Stegen is also two years younger than his competitor, though his career has been hampered by injuries.

blocks.caption: Perhaps Marc-André ter Stegen will find his way back into the Germany team via Ajax?Image: Van der Velden/Fotostand/picture alliance

blocks.text: After several serious injuries and a legal dispute with Barcelona, ter Stegen has gone on loan to Ajax, improving his chances of returning between the posts for Germany.

"As far as ter Stegen is concerned, I assume he’ll definitely be in the mix," Lothar Matthäus recently wrote for Sky. "If he continues to perform well in Amsterdam, he's a candidate for the number one spot."
Alexander Nübel: Out of the spotlight in Turkey

Alexander Nübel was Germany's third-string goalkeeper at the World Cup. He had been consistent at Stuttgart but moved to Besiktas this summer, where he has made a strong start. However, former national team goalkeeper Toni Schumacher sees the move as a disadvantage for the 29-year-old.

"His move to Turkey has taken him out of the spotlight," Schumacher, who also played for Fenerbahce for three years during his playing days, told Bild. "It simply has a positive effect when you play in your own country week after week and thrill the fans with your saves."
Loris Karius: History with Klopp at Liverpool
A goalkeeper who has never been called up to the Germany team but shares a history with Jürgen Klopp is Loris Karius.

blocks.caption: Once considered one of Germany's most promising goalkeepers, Loris Karius appears to now, aged 33, have a real chance of being in the Germany set-up Image: Norbert Schmidt/picture alliance

blocks.text: Karius, who has been at Schalke since January 2025, was at times Klopp’s number one at Liverpool. However, he made two critical mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final against Real Madrid and was subsequently dropped.
Back in the Bundesliga aged 33, Karius is now delivering consistent performances and may have played his way back into the spotlight.
"When people associate me with that, it's a testament to the performance I’m putting in. That's great," Karius said recently in an interview with Sky.
Several keepers who could play for Germany or somewhere else

If none of the obvious candidates get selected, there are also a number of other good goalkeepers who might be considered. First among them is Noah Atubolu. The 24-year-old Eintracht Frankfurt keeper, who has Nigerian heritage, was the number one for Germany's U21s from 2022 to 2025, and was called up to the senior squad once last October.

blocks.caption: Finn Dahmen (left) and Noah Atubolu (right) are both young keepers with potentialImage: Sebastian Räppold/Matthias Koch/picture alliance

blocks.text: Freiburg's Mio Backhaus is another promising talent. The 22-year-old’s mother is from Japan, meaning Backhaus is also eligible to play for Japan. He even played for the Japanese U15 team, but has since progressed through Germany's youth teams up to the U21 level.
In addition to Atubolu and Backhaus, there are also Augsburg's Finn Dahmen (28), Stuttgart's Dennis Seimen (20), and Diant Ramaj (24), who left recently relegated Heidenheim to join Copenhagen.

If Klopp wants to rely on one of the five, it might be worth playing them sooner rather than later in a competitive game. After all, just like Atubolu and Backhaus, the other three are also eligible to play for another country due to their heritage. Dahmen could also play for England, Seimen for Romania, and Ramaj for Kosovo.
Köpke: 'Develop a young keeper as new number one'
"I think they need to develop a young goalkeeper as the number one right now," Andreas Köpke, the goalkeeper on Germany's 1996 European championship team, told Bild.
Germany's former goalkeeping coach pointed to Bayern's backup goalkeeper Urbig alongside Backhaus and Atubolu—though only as and when Urbig plays regulary at club level.
And given his standing at Bayern, that's bound to come down to how long Manuel Neuer choses to continue to play.
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: Dispatch from the ICC grounds: A waving Duterte, tears of joy, delaying tactics
articles.summary: Just after the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III adjourned the third status conference for Rodrigo Duterte"s upcoming trial, the former president looked out and waved at viewers in…

blocks.text: THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Just after the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III adjourned the third status conference for Rodrigo Duterte’s upcoming trial, the former president looked out and waved at viewers in the public gallery.
The gesture lasted only a few seconds as the gallery curtain closed, leaving several Duterte supporters tearing up.

Unlike previous hearings in Duterte’s ICC case, only a few supporters attended today’s status conference, as they did not expect the former president to appear today. The other viewers were students touring the ICC, a handful of journalists, and other local visitors.
“Looking good”
The conference started promptly at 10:30 AM local time (4:30 PM Manila), with the gallery curtain slowly opening up.

From our position in the media seats, Duterte was on the far end of the defense side. My journalist colleagues and I had been anticipating his appearance since there was no publicized request from his counsel, Peter Haynes, to waive his attendance before the court.
As the judges entered the courtroom, Duterte was seated with his right hand on his chin – a posture reminiscent of one of his presidential portraits.

Before the prosecution began their presentation, the journalists had a good five minutes spent observing the former president – who, as the photos of the day show, sports long hair and dons a black jacket and white inner shirt – before leaving the gallery to break the news.
For some journalists, he was “looking good”, far from a mental image of an emaciated Duterte that his relatives had described some months back.

A photojournalist, whom I briefly spoke with as I left the gallery, described Duterte as “looking happy” when she saw him entering the courtroom. She said the former president “invited” them to go to “our beautiful country of the Philippines.”
“Tears of joy”
When we returned to the gallery, I saw some smiling supporters locking their gaze on the former president, while others clasped their hands, as if praying.
Janet Suliman, a long-time Duterte supporter, said she cried “tears of joy” when she saw Duterte – his first public appearance before the Court since March 14, 2025.
She and other supporters told me they had expected him to appear in a wheelchair or in a visibly worse condition.

“He’s a fighter,” Suliman said. “He looked confident. We believe he knows that he didn’t do anything wrong.” She added that they would continue to stand by Duterte “until the end” and that “justice would prevail.”
I told Suliman that the relatives of drug war victims also want that justice as well. However, she said that some killed during the drug war “fought back” against the police.

Other supporters, Cecil van Hameren, Alma Knoester, Jennifer Carcueba and Alvin Sarzate, questioned the volume of evidence the prosecution presented after Duterte’s defense said its evidence list had grown to nearly 20,000 items.
They described the number as “unbelievable” and questioned how prosecutors could have gathered and prepared such a large amount of material.
“Magician,” one supporter said, referring to the prosecution.
Others dismissed the evidence as “made up” and “nonsense.”

The prosecution has maintained that its evidence supports the charges against Duterte, while his defense team has raised separate concerns about the volume and organization of the material disclosed in the case.
Delaying tactic

The Duterte Panagutin Network (DPN) and other critics of the former president likewise anticipated his first appearance in court – but they rejected claims from his lawyers about his health and fitness to stand trial.

Although none of the DPN members watched the conference in the gallery, they told me during their protest outside the ICC grounds that they would stay tuned, considering Duterte’s appearance before the court was already a “big win” for the relatives of drug war victims who yearn to hold him accountable.

Fiona Magallanes of Bayan Netherlands and convenor of Panagutin Network Netherlands wrote in a statement that Duterte’s health arguments were his camp’s “delaying tactic”. She said the group hopes to see him appear again when his trial starts, which has been scheduled on November 30.
"Duterte's appearance in court today proves he has been feigning sick all this time. It was all a delaying tactic, delaying justice and delaying healing for the victims’ families,” she said.
Magallanes also said Duterte “looks well,” which she claimed was “exposing the myth that his camp has continuously pushed of a sickly old man supposedly ‘unfit to stand trial.’”

Duterte’s lawyers have argued before the ICC that he suffers from cognitive impairment affecting his memory and ability to participate meaningfully in the proceedings. The Trial Chamber has yet to rule on his fitness to stand trial.
Planned demonstrations

The next status conference, based on the ICC court calendar, is scheduled for October 13. Duterte’s supporters told me they are gearing up for protests leading up to the November 30 trial. The Netherlands-based Duterte Panagutin Network, meanwhile, has already scheduled demonstrations on the first day of the trial. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Gaza: 20 dead, including children, in building collapse
articles.summary: The search for survivors has been hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery in the Gaza Strip. Authorities say 2,000 damaged buildings in the territory are occupied by families who have…

image.caption: The search for survivors is ongoing but hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machineryImage: Mahmoud Issa/REUTERS

blocks.text: At least 20 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave.

"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found.

"My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home."
The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues.
Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse

"The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people ​are digging with their bare hands."
With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory.
"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter."

According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents.

"Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian ⁠Coordinator for ​the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
"No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter."
Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery
Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave.

Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians.

More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed.

articles.title: Lanao del Sur governor backs Macacua’s continued leadership in BARMM
articles.summary: ILIGAN CITY— Lanao del Sur Gov. Mamintal Adiong Jr. has expressed his support for the continued leadership of Abdulraof Macacua as chief minister of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim…

blocks.text: ILIGAN CITY— Lanao del Sur Gov. Mamintal Adiong Jr. has expressed his support for the continued leadership of Abdulraof Macacua as chief minister of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) following the region’s first parliamentary elections.
Adiong, who also serves as secretary-general of the BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC), congratulated Macacua on what he described as his “decisive victory” in the historic elections held on Sept. 14.

The first regular Bangsamoro parliamentary elections filled 80 seats in the region’s regular parliament. Under the parliamentary system, the chief minister will be chosen by the newly elected parliament rather than directly by voters.

“I extend my warmest congratulations to Chief Minister Abdulraof ‘Sammy Gambar’ Macacua on his decisive victory in the historic first Bangsamoro parliamentary elections, and I am glad to reaffirm my personal and political support for his continued leadership as Chief Minister of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao,” Adiong said.
Adiong said he and Macacua had worked together in building the Bangsamoro region, including in regional governance and public service.
He said he has long believed that the region’s future would be better served by leaders who can build bridges across political differences.

“I know his sincerity, his discipline, and his love for the Bangsamoro, and I am confident that under his leadership, this new chapter of self-governance will be guided with wisdom and unity,” Adiong said.
He also said he believed his support for Macacua was shared by local leaders in Lanao del Sur.
As governor, Adiong said the province is ready to work with the Bangsamoro government under Macacua’s leadership to advance programs benefiting communities across the region.
Macacua’s Bangsamoro Federalist Party garnered 31 of 80 seats in the incoming regular Parliament, short of the number needed to form the regional government.

Adiong’s recent pronouncement raises the possibility that the BGC could form a coalition with the BFP, throwing its eight seats behind Macacua, along with six more seats won by his local party, SIAP. /mcm

articles.title: Previously unseen drawings by Moomins author Tove Jansson to go on show in London
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Exhibition focussing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins book

The Moomin books about lovable trolls with hippopotamus…

blocks.text: The Moomin books about lovable trolls with hippopotamus snouts who live in harmony with nature are a global publishing phenomenon, having sold up to 30m copies since the Finnish artist and writer Tove Jansson wrote and illustrated them between 1945 and 1977.
Now previously unseen drawings of her eccentric characters will be among more than 100 exhibits in a major exhibition that is being staged in London 25 years after her death.
Tove Jansson and her Families will open at the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration in November, it will be announced on Thursday.
Billed as the UK’s first exhibition to focus on Jansson’s illustrations, it will feature sketches, photographs and films, as well as her correspondence with those closest to her and fans of all ages.

blocks.caption: Tove Jansson ‘had this very special skill to harness themes that touch the reader’, said her niece, Sophia Jansson.  Photograph: Eva Konikoff

blocks.text: The displays will include original art from her first published book, The Moomins and the Great Flood, in which she presented a world “where everything was natural and benign – and possible”, in a story about Moomintroll’s search, with Moominmamma, for their missing Moominpappa and how they found their way to the magical Moominvalley.

Jansson’s books celebrate nature, friendship, tolerance and the freedom to be oneself. Enchanting children and adults alike, they have been translated into more than 60 languages, inspiring animated films, television series and theme parks.

blocks.caption: A sketch of Moominpappa with a giant shell has not been shown before.  Photograph: Moomin Characters

blocks.text: Sophia Jansson, Tove’s niece, told the Guardian: “She had this very special skill to harness themes that touch the reader … on a universal and a personal level – and then disguise them in these stories, so that we think we’re reading about Moomins in Moominvalley and, when you finish the book, you realise that you’re actually reading about ‘us’, about humans and how we interact and all our peculiarities.”

Previously unseen material will include a sketch of Moominpappa, a sea-loving adventurer, with a giant shell. It was an early draft for the cover of Moominpappa at Sea, in which the Moomin family moves to a remote island at the mercy of the sea and storms.

It is among images that even Sophia, the creative director of the Moomins Characters brand, has not seen before, but which have recently come to light: “This is the amazing thing about Tove. She was extremely prolific.”

Asked whether this is the first-ever UK exhibition to focus on Jansson’s illustrations, Sophia said: “Definitely, because the one in Dulwich [Picture Gallery in 2017] was mainly to show her paintings.”

Paul Gravett, a Jansson expert and guest curator at the Quentin Blake Centre, told the Guardian: “The prose novels are still extremely topical because of the sheer variety of characters that are brought together. They are filled with a lot of love and tolerance, that ‘isn’t it wonderful how very different we all are?’
“Moomin celebrates that, enjoying eccentricity and going with the flow of life. This is one of the reasons that they’re not just for children. They have a lot of depth to them.”
Gravett said the draft book cover was different from the one eventually published, but “every bit as good”.

At the age of seven, Jansson was already writing and illustrating homemade booklets, which she sold to her classmates. Exhibits will include these drawings. “You can see a lot of the same fascination with fantasy and dreams, which came out of her childhood reading,” Gravett said.

Her passion for fantasy literature stayed with her. She illustrated Swedish editions of Lewis Carroll’s The Hunting of the Snark and Alice in Wonderland in a horror style. With JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit, she reinterpreted his characters, making Gollum monstrously large.

blocks.caption: Jansson’s books have been translated into more than 60 languages. Photograph: Moomin Characters

blocks.text: Tolkien himself was surprised. Realising he had never clarified Gollum’s size, he amended the second edition to describe him as “a small, slimy creature”. The first English edition with Jansson’s illustrations will be published this month by HarperCollins.

Jansson was an outspoken political cartoonist, criticising fascism during the second world war, once saying: “Most of all I liked the fact that I got to be beastly to Hitler and Stalin.” In one cartoon, she depicted a woman and little girl in a toy shop with the caption: “Don’t you have a doll that says ‘Momma’?/ ‘No, little friend, our new stock says ‘Heil Hitler!’”

She had a special connection with London: at a time when it was rare for female cartoonists to have their own daily strip, her first Moomin series went into print from 1954 in London’s Evening News. Her comic strips were circulated worldwide.

Exhibits will include a sketch for one of the earliest examples. Gravett said: “It’s a miracle it survived because it’s covered in coffee stains and it was headed for the waste paper bin. A fellow cartoonist spotted it and rescued it.”
Gravett is working on a Jansson book, following his 2022 study of her illustration work.

items: Tove Jansson and her Families runs from 21 November to 9 May at the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration, Clerkenwell, London

articles.title: Bondi attacks prompt creation of new institute for emergency care of children in NSW
articles.summary:
NSW Institute for Paediatric Trauma will help doctors, researchers and specialists prepare for trauma cases

  • Get our

blocks.text: A new institute dedicated to improving emergency medical care for severely injured children will be established in New South Wales following recent high-profile trauma events in the state.

Based at the Sydney Children’s hospital in Randwick, the NSW Institute for Paediatric Trauma will bring together clinicians, researchers and specialists to deliver advanced training and simulations across the health system.
Expected to be operational within six months, the institute aims to prepare medical teams for complex paediatric trauma cases, from initial emergency treatment to long-term rehabilitation.
The NSW health minister, Ryan Park, said the initiative follows emergency responses to critical incidents in the state.

“The events that occurred at Bondi Beach and at Bondi Junction have forever left their mark on NSW,” Park said. “Seeing the way in which our frontline workers and clinicians responded to these events with such courage and professionalism was nothing short of remarkable.”
“We know we won’t always be able to prevent trauma events, but we can make sure we are ready to respond when children and families need us most.”
Medical experts stress that treating children requires distinct clinical approaches to treating adults.
Dr Guy Henry, co-director of trauma services at Randwick, said children’s bodies, injuries and clinical needs differ significantly from adult patients.

While adult trauma frequently involves assaults or motor vehicle accidents, paediatric admissions generally present distinct patterns, including internal organ injuries in adolescents taking physical risks, and a growing number of e-bike crashes.

“Burns is another issue with children, there’s a different pattern of burns in children compared to adults,” he said. “People need to be aware of the differences and need to know how to respond to those differences.”
Preparing for mass casualties

Henry, who attended to victims of the Westfield Bondi Junction stabbings in 2024 and the Bondi beach terror attack, said regular education and mass casualty simulations are essential for building response capabilities.

He cited the medical response to the 2017 Manchester Arena attack – where hospital staff had completed a mass casualty simulation six weeks before – as evidence of how practice improves outcomes during critical events.
after newsletter promotion

“Through education, including the use of simulation, we can make people more familiar with managing trauma, with something like a mass casualty that no one might have any experience with,” Henry said.
“We get people more familiar, a little bit more comfortable, and that will then make us improve on how we manage things.”

Training will initially be based at Randwick, with future plans to explore how the program can be expanded across regional NSW and into the ACT, which regularly transfers paediatric trauma cases to Sydney hospitals.
The institute also aims to extend education simulation training to pre-hospital first responders, including paramedics, firefighters, police and the State Emergency Service.
Beyond clinical care and injury prevention research, the institute will address the psychological toll on healthcare workers and affected families.

“It’s been identified that not only do we have the child that we have to manage, we have the families to manage, we also have our own staff to manage,” Henry said, noting that upskilling staff helps lessen the psychological trauma of critical events.

The institute will draw on expertise across the Sydney Children’s Hospitals Network – including the children’s hospital at Westmead and the Newborn and Paediatric Emergency Transport Service – and will complement the Agency for Clinical Innovation’s Institute of Trauma and Injury Management. Philanthropic support will be provided through the Sydney Children’s Hospitals Foundation.

articles.title: Amazon to launch Ring ‘neighbourhood watch’ app in UK amid US privacy fears
articles.summary:
Doorbell firm aims to replace WhatsApp or Facebook groups with platform where people can post about safety or lost pets

Amazon’s doorbell camera maker Ring is to launch its Neighbours…

blocks.text: Amazon’s doorbell camera maker Ring is to launch its Neighbours community app in the UK in an attempt to supplant neighbourhood WhatsApp or Facebook groups.
The service is intended as a modern equivalent of a community message board, where neighbours can post about safety, community matters or lost pets.
It is being made available free of charge inside the existing Ring app for UK users from 21 October and can be used by anyone, regardless of whether they own one of the brand’s products.

“We used to have the village noticeboard, but as things have changed we no longer have that local connection,” said Dave Ward, the managing director of international for Ring. “Instead what you see in WhatsApp or other services is quite a broad-stroked flood of information, the bins being left out, that sort of thing. It’s a big group that ends up getting muted.
“We’re trying to tailor this down to just the things that really matter to your immediate community and then it becomes super useful.”
Those who join the service set their address and a radius of between 0.1 and five miles to join the local community.

Some of the more controversial features of the Neighbours service from the US will not be immediately available in the UK. That includes the Neighbours Verified service, which allows entities and services such as the local fire brigade to post advisory messages to local communities.

The Community Requests feature, which allows the police to issue calls for footage from Ring cameras in a local area in response to incidents, has drawn the most ire from privacy campaigners. It allows those with footage of incidents to share it with the police on an opt-in and per-event basis. The police are not informed of those that choose not to share footage.
Both features are being developed for release in the UK but not until later this year at the earliest.

Neighbours will launch with basic anonymised posting narrowed into categories, which must conform to a strict set of guidelines barring illegal content, discrimination, speculation or multiple other conditions.
The posts are moderated by AI and humans before and after being published. Content can be shared from Ring doorbells and other cameras.
after newsletter promotion

“We are going to coach people to make sure they’re creating the right sort of post, asking them if that’s really something they want to write or whether it really need that descriptive term, to help stop the type of content no one wants to see and make it more community focused. That’s very different to other places [such as WhatsApp groups],” Ward said.
Amazon bought the video doorbell and home security camera maker in 2018 in a deal reportedly worth more than $1bn.
The new service will also have a feature called “Search Party for Dogs”, which allows users of lost pets to post an image and report of a lost dog.

Those in the neighbourhood who have Ring cameras and a suitable cloud subscription can opt in to join the search. They will then be notified if their cameras see a dog, prompted to check whether it is the correct dog, and then can optionally notify and share the video with the pet owner.

In an attempt to negate some privacy fears, Ring recently announced a new default encryption mechanism for camera footage called TAKE (throw away the key encryption). This feature provides Ring’s systems time-limited keys to the recordings, blocking the company and others access to the videos after 24 hours. Further processing or access, including by law enforcement, requires user consent to issue replacement 24-hour keys from the user’s Ring app.

articles.title: How the Houthis are also putting Egypt under pressure
articles.summary: The Houthis, a Yemeni rebel group, are expanding their control of maritime corridors in the Red Sea area. Their target is their avowed enemy Saudi Arabia. But the military moves also endanger Egypt.

image.caption: Waterway under pressure: the Suez Canal, here near Egypt's Ismailia provinceImage: Ahmed Gomaa/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Any and all ships may pass, at least at first. That was how the spokesperson for Yemen's Houthis rebel militia put it. Transit through the Red Sea would be safe, with one exception: According to the Houthi spokesperson, ships from Saudi Arabia would not be allowed to pass this stretch of the sea.

The comments came during a time when the Houthi militia has been fighting to increase its presence at the southern entrance to the ocean passage. The Houthis now control the tiny volcanic island of Mayun, also known as Perim, at the entrance to the Red Sea, as well as other parts of the Yemeni coast and some small islands.
With these moves, pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia, the country that opposes the Houthis and previously fought a war (unsuccessfully) with them.
Red Sea strains rattle energy markets
But pressure is now also increasing in Egypt. Every decrease in shipping traffic through the Red Sea also impacts one of that country's most important sources of national income, the Suez Canal.

As yet, maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has not been significantly reduced. According to news agency Reuters, last Saturday 24 ships passed through it and on Sunday, 27 did so. That is around the same as the 10-day average. The Houthis appear to want to signal that their plan is not stop traffic altogether. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a chokepoint between Yemen and and the Horn of Africa. Ships have to pass it to enter the Red Sea.

blocks.caption: Boats that are not Saudi Arabian can still pass the Bab al-Mandeb Strait (file photo from April 2026)Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: In general though, maritime traffic has decreased here, according to maritime intelligence organization Kpler. On Monday, 21 ships went through the strait. But in the middle of July, the average number of ships passing through was 47.
How will things develop from here?

"The Houthis could actually interrupt, or at least significantly disturb, the connection between Asia and Europe," says Stephan Roll, a senior fellow with the Africa and Middle East division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, or SWP, in Berlin. "So first we have to wait and see how big the actual disruption to the Suez Canal will be."
Even complete control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait doesn't automatically mean control of the Suez Canal. But it does give the Houthis a further opportunity to indirectly threaten traffic.

For Egypt, this new disruption comes at a particularly unwelcome time. Houthi attacks at the end of 2023 had already disrupted business at the Suez Canal. According to the International Monetary Fund, earnings at the canal in 2024 fell by around $6 billion (€5.2 billion). Before the current security crisis, Egypt had been making between $9 billion and $10 billion from the Suez Canal annually.
More recently things had actually been improving again.
"The situation is certainly problematic compared to 2023," Roll told DW. "But it is not so clearly negative compared to the situation one, two or even three months ago."

blocks.caption: Important source of income: opening of the Suez Canal in 1869Image: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thanks to rising oil prices and the resulting higher cost of circumnavigating Africa, shipping companies had been using the Red Sea as they travelled between Asia and Europe.

The Suez Canal's finances had recently improved. The Suez Canal Authority, which manages the passage, reported that during the 2025-2026 fiscal year, revenues had risen by 23% to $4.67 billion (€4.5 billion). Despite the various conflicts in the region, this actually represented a recovery for the Suez Canal.
Houthi offensive could change all that

There is also a second critical factor. After recent drone attacks that the Saudis blamed on Iraqi groups, Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline to the coastal city of Yanbu will be out of service for at least several weeks. Between 4 million and 5 million barrels of oil were going through the 1,200 kilometer pipeline per day as the Saudis attempted to circumnavigate the Strait of Hormuz, blocked due to the US-Iran war. This latest damage could put as much as 4% of global supply at risk, according to Reuters.

An analysis by Qatar-based think tank, the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, warns of a scenario where the Persian Gulf and Red Sea are both likely to become more precarious. The East Asia Institute, a think tank based in Korea, has also written about the dangers of dual choke points.
Neither route can be seen as an independent alternative because flows of oil and trade depend on secure connections at several points.
Certainly for Egypt, this will increase economic pressure.
What can Egypt do about this?
In geopolitical terms, there is not a lot that Egypt can do. The Houthis in Yemen have only impacted the country indirectly.
"Egypt's military capabilities are very limited," Steffen Krüger, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation's Cairo office, explained.

Egyptian interventions in Yemen in the 1960s are still remembered in Cairo — back then, the country sent thousands of troops to support a new government in Yemen, in a war that would eventually last years — so Egypt would prefer to exercise restraint there.
"Although Egypt formally remains a member of the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis, its participation is largely symbolic," Krüger told DW.
And there is no doubt that Egyptian officials have noted the lack of success other countries like Saudi Arabia and the US have had in their attempts to rein in the Houthis.

"The Egyptians simply have no real alternative," argues the SWP's Roll, adding that Egypt is likely to try diplomacy first. "Basically they have to try to put a positive spin on a bad situation and somehow negotiate appropriate arrangements with the Houthis."

That may already be happening. According to London-based media outlet The New Arab on September 14, the Houthis offered to talk directy to Cairo about shipping security via the International Chamber of Shipping in London. The same publication said Egypt had rejected the offer for fear of it being seen as recognizing Houthi authority.

blocks.caption: The Strait of Hormuz has also been dangerous: This week the Panama-flagged El Gaia tanker was hit, although it is unclear by whomImage: IRIB/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Tuesday, Saudi Arabian leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, travelled to Cairo to try to get Egypt's support against the Houthis.
"The Egyptians are likely to wait and see," says Roll of the SWP about the next steps for Cairo.

Egypt has a difficult balancing act to perform. The country is closely allied with Saudi Arabia but is also bound to suffer economically in any further escalation between the Saudis and the Houthi group.

A decisive factor will depend on if, and how, the Houthis restrict maritime shipping, and if they go beyond vessels with Saudi Arabian ties, or whether they are just using their currenty improved military position to exert pressure on their enemies.
This story was originally published in German.

articles.title: ICC orders Rodrigo Duterte’s continued detention
articles.summary: 'The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions,' says the order issued by the ICC Trial Chamber III

blocks.text: DUTERTE. Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court, as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, on September 16 2026.
Piroschka van de Wouw/Pool via Reuters
'The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions,' says the order issued by the ICC Trial Chamber III
MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III ordered the continued detention of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte at The Hague, Netherlands.

“The Chamber therefore finds no notable change in circumstances that warrant the release of the Accused, with or without conditions. For these reasons, the chamber hereby decides that the accused shall continue to be detained,” said the chamber’s decision on Wednesday, September 16.
In May, the chamber said Duterte is still not qualified to avail himself of temporary liberty, ruling that the former president shall continue to be detained.

At the ICC, chambers conduct a yearly review to check if detention is still warranted for an accused. Specifically, the judges will check for changed circumstances that would warrant temporary liberty for detained suspects.
After the May resolution, the chamber reviewed Duterte’s continued detention again.
According to the trial chamber, it found that there’s a likelihood that Duterte would “abscond,” “obstruct,” or “endanger” the court proceedings.

“In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the Prosecution’s submission of the Witness and Evidence Lists (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases the Accused’s ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” the court explained.

The court is also assessing Duterte’s fitness for trial. But even though the results of this assessment are still pending, the “panel’s reports do not contain any information that warrants a modification of the accused’s detention,” the court said.

Under the Rome Statute, which created the ICC, a suspect cannot be released if they present risk factors, which include the danger of fleeing, obstructing justice by intimidating witnesses, or recommitting the same alleged crimes.

blocks.caption: Rodrigo Duterte attends ICC hearing in person for the first time

blocks.text: “Accordingly, the Chamber finds that the risks under Article 58(1)(b)(i) and (ii) have increased and, in respect of the risks outlined in Article 58(1)(b)(iii), sees no change in circumstances,” the court explained.

The chamber held the third status conference on Duterte’s case on Wednesday, where the parties discussed the possible evidence for the upcoming November 30 trial. Duterte appeared during the hearing, marking his first personal appearance before the court since his arrest in March 2025. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte to remain detained - ICC trial chamber
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has unanimously decided to keep former President Rodrigo Duterte detained.

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published September 16, 2026 9:46pm

Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte appears before the International Criminal Court, as the court hears arguments regarding Duterte's health and ability to stand trial, while he faces murder charges related to his war on drugs, in The Hague, Netherlands, September 16, 2026. REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw/Pool
THE HAGUE – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has unanimously decided to keep former President Rodrigo Duterte detained.

In a decision released shortly after the conclusion of the third status conference, the Chamber found a likelihood of Duterte “absconding and/or obstructing or endangering the investigation or the court proceedings.”

“In respect of the latter considerations, owing to the Prosecution’s submission of the Witness and Evidence Lists, (thereby disclosing the identities of the witnesses and the contents of their expected testimony), this increases the Accused’s ability to interfere with witnesses, either directly or through his family or supporters in the Philippines,” the decision read.
The Chamber noted it has yet to decide on the issue of Duterte’s fitness, as the defense’s requested “greater medical certainty” while challenging the expert panel’s report.

However, the Chamber said the observations of Duterte’s lawyers “do not provide any information that constitutes new facts or a change in circumstances” which would warrant a modification of his detention. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Reform-linked thinktank ‘to call for big tax cuts for the rich’
articles.summary:
Centre for a Better Britain will urge abolishing inheritance tax and phasing out capital gains tax, report says

A thinktank linked to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK is preparing an influential…

blocks.text: A thinktank linked to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK is preparing an influential policy plan that is reportedly going to call for substantial tax cuts for the rich.

The Centre for a Better Britain (CFABB) is due to publish the 200-page document next week, giving insight into the economic and financial policies that are likely to form part of Reform UK’s platform before the next election.

The thinktank proposals are said to benefit some of the UK’s wealthiest taxpayers, by abolishing inheritance tax and phasing out capital gains tax, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.

That would mean depriving the Treasury of a lucrative source of funding. The UK’s inheritance tax raised £8.5bn last year, while capital gains tax brought in a record £24bn in 2024-25, for public and government operations.

The CFABB – founded by the former Reform chief operations officer Jonathan Brown – is also expected to propose cutting rules and regulation for the UK’s financial services sector, in what is being dubbed “Big Bang 2.0”, a reference to Margaret Thatcher’s City deregulation drive in the 1980s.
That is on top of calls to break up the Treasury and move its economic growth responsibilities to a different department, the news outlet reported.

A spokesperson for the CFABB said Bloomberg appeared to have been briefed on an “early draft of the report” that did not reflect what would be released next week. They also insisted that there would be “no unfunded tax cuts” proposed in the report, and “no suggestions that we go pre-2008” in terms of regulatory reforms.
The spokesperson said the Bloomberg story included inaccuracies, but said they would not be drawn into discussing which points were incorrect.

The prospective tax proposals come as Reform UK faces questions over the motivation of two crypto billionaires – Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne – who each donated £36m to the party within 24 hours last weekend. The donations, totalling a combined £72m, amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics. Harborne and Delo have both denied seeking to buy influence over the party’s policies.
The CFABB has notable ties with Farage’s party, with its operations based in Millbank Tower near Reform’s headquarters.

It formally launched as CFABB in September last year, after raising fresh funds under its previous guise, Resolute 1850. The original name is said to have been reference to the Royal Navy ship, HMS Resolute, whose timbers were used to make the US president’s desk in the Oval Office.
after newsletter promotion

In an interview with the Financial Times last autumn, Brown – the thinktank’s founder – said he planned to look at ways to weaken the authority of Britain’s courts and civil service, in what some said echoed “Project 2025”, the US project drawn up in the run-up to Donald Trump’s second presidency to help him deliver radical conservative policies with greater political power.
CFABB currently has five staff, and previously counted James Orr – Reform UK’s former head of policy – as chair of its advisory board.

Orr was suspended from Reform UK earlier this month after being filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to help orchestrate a plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. Orr denies wrongdoing.
A spokesperson for CFABB said Orr stepped down from the thinktank role when he took a job at Reform in February, and was not replaced.

articles.title: Saudis pound Yemen as Houthis solidify gains in new Middle East war front
articles.summary: Saudi warplanes pounded Yemen, the Houthis said on Wednesday, as the Iran-backed fighters solidified their gains after a lightning advance that has extended Tehran's reach in the Middle East war and…

image.caption: Men ride in the back of a pickup truck during a mass funeral procession for Houthi officers and other military personnel in Sanaa, Yemen, on Wednesday. (The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

Saudi warplanes pounded Yemen, the Houthis said on Wednesday, as the Iran-backed fighters solidified their gains after a lightning advance that has extended Tehran's reach in the Middle East war and further disrupted global oil supplies.
Houthis recently swept through Yemeni towns along the Red Sea coast, seized islands

Saudi warplanes pounded Yemen and Houthi fighters launched drones and missiles at Saudi cities, the Iran-backed movement said Wednesday, after a lightning advance that has extended Tehran's reach in the Middle East war.

In a sign of the worsening conflict in a new theatre, the United States tightened its travel warning for Saudi Arabia, banning government employees from travelling within 32 kilometres of the Yemen border.

The Houthis, who since last week have swept through Yemeni towns along the Red Sea coast and seized islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at its mouth, released battlefield video overnight of fighters seizing armoured vehicles from Saudi-backed forces. Warplanes flew overhead and huge explosions billowed into the sky from desert dunes, the video showed.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had launched fresh drone and missile strikes on the major Saudi Red Sea oil port of Yanbu, and at a southern Saudi airbase at Khamis Mushait. He did not say when the strikes had taken place.
Both cities were among a wide range of locations where Saudi Arabia announced alerts on Tuesday, although there were no similar announcements on Wednesday.
Saudi officials and oil company Aramco did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
Earlier, Saree said the Houthis had also shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet. No immediate evidence was presented of that incident.
Houthi rebel control expands over key oil shipping lane

Saree said the Saudis had carried out as many as 450 airstrikes on Yemen this week. Officials in the Saudi-backed government that controls southern Yemen have acknowledged that their forces and those of Saudi Arabia were conducting airstrikes on Houthi positions, though Riyadh itself has not confirmed them.

The Houthis have fired repeatedly into Saudi Arabia over the past week, causing alarms over cities in the south and west. An attack blamed on Iran-aligned fighters in Iraq last week also knocked out Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the main route used to divert oil exports from the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Riyadh said its air defences had shot down a Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, an attack it said crossed a "red line" of threatening shrines sacred to all Muslims.
Houthi spokesperson Saree denied the group had targeted Mecca, and said the Saudi reports were a setup for propaganda purposes.

Sources told Reuters that U.S. officials had held a meeting with the Houthis over the weekend in Oman, at which the group said it had no intention of attacking American vessels and was committed to a ceasefire reached with the U.S. last year.
Danger of global energy supply shortage worsening

The extension of the war into Yemen threatens to worsen the global energy supply shortage caused by the six-month-old U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The price of Brent crude hovered around $108 US a barrel on Wednesday, close to its highest level since May. The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the United States hit another all-time high above $6.30 US a gallon for the first time.

Traders say a prolonged closure of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline could cut off as much as four per cent of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia has not said when operations might resume, but U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday that crude oil should be flowing through the pipeline within days.

items: Houthis attack more Saudi targets as regional talks with Iran postponed
Houthis seize strategic island, Saudis close pipeline as fighting escalates

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years, but reignited when the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in July and fired at southern areas in the kingdom. Violence has intensified sharply this month when the militant group pushed back forces aligned with the Saudi-backed internationally recognized Yemeni government.
Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned U.S. President Donald Trump last week seeking military support, which so far has been limited to intelligence aid.
The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in 2025, but halted that campaign after reaching what Trump described as a ceasefire that would halt attacks on ships.

Trump now faces a dilemma of whether to stand by and risk the Houthi advance worsening the global energy crisis, or provide more direct military support to the Saudis and risk extending the costly U.S. intervention to another theatre.

articles.title: Suffolk police release footage of Noah Woods as search for missing boy continues
articles.summary:
Hundreds of volunteers join hunt for three-year-old who went missing on Tuesday afternoon

A massive search operation is under way in and around a Suffolk village for a missing three-year-old…

blocks.text: A massive search operation is under way in and around a Suffolk village for a missing three-year-old boy with autism, supported by hundreds of volunteers.
Suffolk police have said the hunt for Noah Woods remains a missing persons investigation with no indication anything sinister has happened.

Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and partially deaf, went missing after a visit to a play area in the village of Brantham on Tuesday afternoon when he became separated from a relative. Police have said Noah will not respond to his name if called.

blocks.caption: Suffolk police release video of Noah Woods before disappearance

blocks.text: In an update on Wednesday, Supt Tom Pearse from Suffolk police said: “This is being treated as a missing person investigation at this stage and there is nothing to indicate anything sinister or any element of criminality has taken place although we keep an open mind as to the circumstances.”
The force released new CCTV stills and footage of the little boy in the play area in Merriam Close just before he vanished.
It is thought that he ran down an alleyway beside the playground towards a nearby new-build housing estate.
The surrounding area includes woods and a pond and is near the River Stour and a railway.
Noah is white with curly ginger hair and was wearing a white T-shirt featuring the TV character Bluey, shorts, and black Vans trainers with a white stripe.

blocks.caption: Volunteers gather at Brantham leisure centre as police officers continue their search for the three-year-old. Photograph: Will Colebourne/PA

blocks.text: On Wednesday, volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre.
They are part of a massive search operation led by police, fire, coastguard and search and rescue teams, with sniffer dogs being used and a helicopter flying overhead.
As well as the ground search, officers are looking at CCTV and other available video footage, going door to door and carrying out aerial and thermal imaging searches.
Noah’s father posted on social media asking volunteers to widen their search beyond the village where possible.
He wrote: “I cannot go another night knowing he’s out there alone, please don’t give up on him guys. He is out there somewhere and I appreciate every single one of you.”

blocks.caption: Supt Tom Pearse speaks to volunteers at Brantham leisure centre. Photograph: Will Colebourne/PA

blocks.text: In the update from police on Wednesday, Pearse urged volunteers to report to the coordination centre and to avoid the railway and open water, which need specialist searching.
He said: “It has now been around 24 hours since Noah was reported as missing to us and we are doing everything we can to find him.

“We are extremely grateful for the support shown by the public. If you are helping please report into the coordination centre to ensure the search continues to be done in a systematic and coordinated fashion.
“This will ensure we can carefully plan and take account of people supporting the search.

“We politely ask people to avoid open waters and railways – these are areas that require specialist and professional expertise. We also ask that personal drones are not used as these can interfere with specialist search equipment.
“There may also be times when officers may need to restrict access to certain areas or move away from search locations.
“Please do not be offended if this happens; it is necessary to allow us to carry out our inquiries and search activity as effectively as possible.”

Advice from Brantham parish council to volunteers included: “You are looking for a frightened three-year-old. Think about slight movements in your peripheral [vision], high and low, tiny small spaces use all your senses whilst searching.”
They have been told not to grab or approach Noah if they find him, but instead to call police on 999 immediately and give their exact location using the What3Words app.

Anyone with private CCTV or doorbell cameras in the village, or who was driving through the area with a dashcam is asked to review the footage from 3pm on Tuesday afternoon onwards for any possible sightings of Noah.

articles.title: Witness: Marcoleta's donors provided funds for his 2025 Senate campaign
articles.summary: The three individuals who donated money to then Sagip party-list Rep. Rodante Marcoleta did so to support his possible 2025 Senate candidacy, a witness from the Office of the Ombudsman told the…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 9:31pm

The three individuals who donated money to then Sagip party-list Rep. Rodante Marcoleta did so to support his possible 2025 Senate candidacy, a witness from the Office of the Ombudsman told the anti-graft court.

Field Investigation Bureau Director Maria Melinda Mananghaya-Henson, citing the Deed of Donation executed by Michael Defensor, Joseph Varias Espiritu and Aristotle Baluyut Viray, made the testimony before the Sandiganbayan Third Division during the hearing on the pending bail petition of Marcoleta.

The Deed of Donation stated that they gave the money to Marcoleta “for and in consideration of my support for the possible candidacy of Donee (Marcoleta) in the May 12, 2025 elections” and that all three Deed of Donation.

Defensor, Espiritu and Viray were all Marcoleta’s co-accused in the P75 million plunder case over Marcoleta’s alleged failure to declare the said P75 million under his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures (SOCE).
During the same hearing, the video of Marcoleta saying that he willfully refused to declare the P75 million campaign donation he received from his donors was played before the anti-graft court.

“Kapag naglagay ako ng figure sa contribution, mapipilitan ako mag-disclose ng pangalan nila dahil mayroon kaakibat na kung tawagin ay deed of acceptance of donation. Papaano iyon? Sabi niya, binigay ko nga sa iyo ‘yan. Ituring mo na lang na utang. Dahil sa hindi ko pwedeng isiwalat ang kanilang identity, kaya sinabi ko, zero in contribution,” Marcoleta said in the video of his television show.

(If I put a figure on their contribution, I would be forced to drop their names due to deed of acceptance of donation. How do I deal with it then? I was told that the money given to me can be treated as a loan. And since I cannot disclose their identity, I stated zero contribution.)
Nelson Lubao, who interviewed Marcoleta during the said November 8, 2025 television episode on Net 25, earlier asked the court to be excused as a witness for the prosecution.

Ahead of Henson’s testimony, prosecution witness Atty. Victoria Kadeja Besinio of the Commission on Elections (Comelec) Political Finance and Affairs Department also testified that Marcoleta, in his position paper submitted to the poll body, said the P75 million formed part of his personal funds.
On Wednesday, the Office of the Ombudsman assured the public that "there is very strong evidence on record that warranted the filing of the case" against Marcoleta and his co-accused. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Iran: Activists sound alarm as regime seizes Baha'i assets
articles.summary: Rights groups warn Iran is increasingly confiscating assets from government critics and members of the country's Baha'i faith, but also actors, athletes, and journalists living abroad.

image.caption: Activists report Iran's security forces taking gold, electronics, tools, wedding rings, and even children's toys during recent home raidsImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: As Washington attempts to intensify economic pressure on Iran, ordinary Iranians face mounting financial distress.

Rights groups say Iranian authorities are increasingly using asset seizures against religious minorities, dissidents and government critics, adding a new layer of economic pressure for people already struggling with soaring living costs.
Members of Iran's Baha'i religious minority seem to be bearing the brunt of the crackdown.

The faith, which originated in 19th-century Persia — now Iran — is not officially recognized by the Islamic Republic. Unlike Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, Baha'is are not protected under Article 13 of Iran's constitution, leaving them vulnerable to longstanding discrimination and persecution.
Baha'is portrayed as 'spies' for Israel
The US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRANA) reported "a wave of arrests, searches of homes and businesses, and seizures of property belonging to Baha'i citizens" at the end of August.

Amnesty International said persecution of the Baha'i community has intensified since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, citing what it described as "a coordinated state campaign of incitement to hostility, violence, discrimination and disinformation falsely accusing Baha'is as spies and collaborators for Israel."

blocks.caption: Bahai activist Padideh Sabeti says Tehran's 'discriminatory practices' deprive Baha'is of the ability to earn a livingImage: privat

blocks.text: "Under current conditions, all people in Iran are facing economic hardship and extremely difficult living conditions, barely putting food on the table for their families," says Padideh Sabeti, spokesperson for the International Baha'i Community.
However, Baha'is suffer even more from the country's economic situation, "as the government's discriminatory practices deprive them of the ability to earn a living," she added.
Sabeti adds that the judiciary uses poverty as leverage, demanding exorbitant bail "which is sometimes equivalent to a hundred years' wages for an average citizen."
Regime goes after prominent critics

The apparatus of repression does not only target religious minorities. The government has announced judiciary orders identifying and seizing assets belonging to over 400 individuals living abroad who authorities described as "supporters of the enemy," including actors, athletes, and overseas journalists.

Domestically, Sadegh Saedinia, manager of the "Saedinia" chain of cafes, received a 12-year prison sentence, a two-year operating ban, and total asset confiscation for posting content related to anti-government protests in Qom, a conservative city considered sacred to Shiites.
The growing number of confiscations has led some observers to ask whether property seizures are also aimed at filling state coffers at a time of economic strain.

blocks.caption: The resources gained through seizures are 'very, very insignificant' compared with Iran's massive budget deficitImage: Privat

blocks.text: The economics of confiscation

Arezoo Karimi, a London-based economic analyst, says the financial impact is likely to be limited. The resources gained through seizures are "very, very insignificant" compared with Iran's massive budget deficit, she said.
According to Karimi, confiscated properties are often auctioned off below market value to individuals with political connections.
Sajjad Khodakarami, a Paris-based journalist, says targeting diaspora dissidents sends a clear psychological warning.
"This tool — which the Islamic Republic previously tested on a segment of society — is now being deployed on a broader scale against its opponents," Khodakarami said.

"Today, this instrument of repression targets not only parts of the Baha'i community, but also various strata of society, including journalists, social and human rights activists, and artists who oppose the ruling political establishment," he added.
"When the Islamic Republic targets the assets of hundreds of people, it sends them a message: Even when you are beyond our physical reach, we will continue to apply pressure on you from all sides."
Toys and wedding rings seized by law enforcement
International human rights monitors reported security forces taking gold, electronics, work tools, wedding rings, and children's toys during recent home raids.
Khodakarami views the confiscation of everyday household items as a dark indicator of the regime's trajectory.

"When government agents stoop so low as to confiscate a couple's wedding rings or a child's toys, it is a sign of barbarism," said Khodakarami. "Moreover, this behavior is not merely a message to the Baha'i community, but a broader warning to all dissidents."

blocks.caption: Khodakarami says post-protest Iran is witnessing 'both the securitization of the economy and the economization of repression'Image: Privat

blocks.text: Khodakarami argues that the government is placing a growing share of the economic burden on ordinary citizens rather than on powerful state institutions.
"As the regime's resources shrink, it tightens the screw on the people's livelihoods," Khodakarami said.
Can Iran avoid hyperinflation?

According to Karimi, the government is relying on money printing and subsidy rollbacks to compensate for declining foreign currency revenues. The analyst warns that current fiscal policies risk pushing the country into galloping inflation.
"On one hand, banks are creating money, while on the other, production is effectively paralyzed," said Karimi.

"If we continue down this path at the current pace, I foresee a day when hyperinflation hits Iran — a day when people pay one fare to commute to work in the morning, but have to pay up to double that for the ride back home, just like what we witnessed in Venezuela and Zimbabwe."

While seizing personal assets may serve as a tool of intimidation and generate limited funds for the security apparatus, analysts say it cannot fix Iran's underlying economic problems and is unlikely to ease the financial pressures facing ordinary Iranians.

articles.title: Magazine from 1894 returned to New Hampshire library after over 130 years
articles.summary:
John Hanson, 84, took advantage of fine amnesty at library to return copy that could’ve amounted to $12,055 in late fees

A current affairs magazine that was checked out from a New Hampshire…

blocks.text: A current affairs magazine that was checked out from a New Hampshire library at the end of the 19th century has finally been returned as a piece of history – more than 130 years overdue.

Staff at Concord Public Library were surprised when an 84-year-old man walked into the branch earlier this month with what NBC News said was “a relatively well-cared-for edition” of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine from September 1894.

John Hanson told the Concord Monitor he took advantage of a fine amnesty at the library to return the publication, avoiding a penalty that could have theoretically amounted to $12,055 in late fees for the 48,220-day loan.
“Yeah, when I saw that, I said to myself: ‘Boy, this would be a good time to bring it back’,” he said.

The person who checked out the magazine, however, is destined to remain unknown. Hanson said it came into his possession during a house move in 1966, and that neither of his parents had a library card.
He said his late first wife, Carol, was a regular library patron, but would never have let an item become even slightly overdue, let alone 1,583 months.

The Century Magazine was an illustrated periodical published between 1881 and 1930 that blended history, literature, poetry and current events. Its heyday was the decades of the late 19th century in which it extensively covered the aftermath of the US civil war.

It also introduced readers to a number of emerging writers such as Henry James and Mark Twain by printing extracts from their works. It carried passages from Twain’s Huckleberry Finn, first published in the US in 1885.
The copy that Hanson returned featured a Concord Public Library bookplate, and advised its borrower that it “may be kept for one week”.

Jennifer Needham, the library’s archivist and outreach coordinator, told the Monitor that she was at the circulation desk when Hanson came in with it. She said he produced it from inside an envelope and told her: “I have a book to return, and I bet you haven’t seen anything like this.”
“I honestly thought it was going to be from the 1980s, 90s or 2000s. But then he pulled this out, and I was like: ‘Ooo, tell me more!’” she said.
“I am just so curious. Like someone obviously checked this out, and why didn’t they bring it back, or did they lose it and then they were ashamed and were afraid to bring it back?”
Articles from the magazine’s September 1894 edition included one covering a debate about the need to provide more outdoor playground space for children at urban public schools.
“That’s one thing that was really interesting,” Needham told NBC.

“I didn’t know this history, that they were arguing that more city schools should have outdoor spaces for children to play. It sounds like during that time, that just wasn’t a priority. It’s interesting that they would play inside then.”
There were also several pages of advertisements for products of the day. One was for Beeman’s Pepsin Gum, touted as “a delicious remedy for all forms of indigestion”.
Another promoted Hernan Cortez Cigars, produced in Key West, Florida, “under the most favorable climatic conditions” to its target audience: “men of brains”.

articles.title: Abortion bans make ‘evidence-based medicine’ impossible in some cases, new report says
articles.summary:
Some 41 states restrict abortions, a ‘core component’ of maternal fetal practice, high-risk pregnancy non-profit says

Maternal fetal specialists should see

blocks.text: Maternal fetal specialists should see abortion care as a “core component” of their practice in states where laws restrict abortion, according to a new special statement from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM).

Some 41 states ban abortion at some point in pregnancy, and these legal restrictions make it difficult or impossible for clinicians to practice “standard-of-care, evidence-based medicine”, the report, released on Tuesday, says.

The Dobbs decision made it even more challenging for patients to access abortion care in the US, as more restrictions went into effect in some states. Deaths from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled between 2020 and 2025, a ProPublica analysis found, and later-abortion providers in haven states report that patients are showing up “later and sicker”.

“In some ways, the practice of maternal-fetal medicine is inseparable from family planning and abortion care,” said Justin Lappen, chair of SMFM’s reproductive health committee and a co-author of the statement.

In July 2021, Kate Dineen was about 33 weeks pregnant and giddy with excitement. Her husband was finally able to join her for his first ultrasound of their second child, after Covid restrictions were loosened. But then the room went quiet; the silence stretched on as the ultrasound tech lingered over images of the baby’s brain. Soon, after an MRI and consultation with a pediatric neurologist, they learned that their son had suffered a catastrophic stroke in utero, and his chances of surviving even the pregnancy were poor.

Dineen remembers asking, “What are my options?” One of the specialists said, “You may still be able to explore termination – if you’re able to travel.” Dineen was stunned. She lived in Massachusetts, where abortions were banned after 24 weeks except in specific cases – and her case didn’t qualify for an exception, she learned. The maternal fetal team at her hospital offered to link her to a later abortion clinic in Washington DC, Dineen said.
She and her husband rushed to find childcare for their 18-month-old son and made the long drive to Maryland, where they stayed multiple nights, to receive care.

“We’re just so grateful to get the compassionate care that we needed and deserved, and should have been able to get closer to home,” Dineen said. If she’d been able to get the abortion in Massachusetts, it would’ve been much easier to grieve and find closure, she said. “Instead, our lives were turned completely upside down,” she said. “I feel like I barely survived it.”

Maternal fetal specialists are at the forefront of many reproductive health decisions – including genetic diagnosis, ultrasound diagnoses and screening for anomalies, and complicated maternal medical conditions. That’s why guidance from professional societies on supporting abortion is key, so providers may expand their roles and “continue to provide as much care as possible” said Lappen.

The statement highlights what can be done on the individual level when it comes to caring for patients, and it points to the role that specialists play in “institutional advocacy” to make sure their health systems have plans to support patients ahead of time, he said.

“It’s really important for health systems, for hospitals, to be able to create safe systems of care and to understand what the state reproductive health legal landscape looks like,” Lappen said. That way, they can create the most comprehensive and expansive systems to provide care, he argued.

It’s imperative to set guidelines now, before emergencies arise, Lappen said. “When someone’s facing a really significant pregnancy complication, where decision-making has to happen in a critically acute or rapid time frame, that’s not the best time to get on the phone with the lawyers.”

Providers and health systems should “expand access to abortion care to the legal limit allowed by state law” to provide the most comprehensive care to patients, the statement says. That means understanding the exceptions to those laws and how providers may offer care in those scenarios, which can often be complicated to interpret but are no less important, Lappen said.
“The law is intended to be sort of black and white,” said Lappen. “And healthcare and physiology and pregnancy complications live in the shades of gray.”

Dineen, who is now an advocate and board member of Reproductive Equity Now, said it’s “really wonderful” for the medical society to highlight the key role that abortion care plays in maternal-fetal medicine.

Providers “should be exploiting exceptions to the fullest extent in ban states”, she said. At the same time, she added, “I wouldn’t want this to be interpreted as ‘bans with exceptions work.’” Maternal-fetal specialists can also advocate against abortion bans in order to serve all of their patients, she said.

It’s a “misconception” that adding exceptions to abortion bans means that patients who need abortions will be able to access them, Dineen said. “A ban with exceptions often functions just as a ban.” Even though she believes her providers wanted to give her the standard of care, and even though Massachusetts did carve out exceptions, she still had to travel hundreds of miles to get an abortion.
In Massachusetts, she said, “we uniquely are able to demonstrate why bans with exceptions don’t result in patients being able to access care.”

In 2022, after Dineen and others testified about how restrictions kept them from medically necessary care, Massachusetts legislators expanded the abortion exception to include “grave fetal diagnoses”. It was an improvement, Dineen said, but some patients were still not getting care. Now, Massachusetts is removing the 24-week ban, which means all patients will have access to standard reproductive care.

The law “unties the hands of our world-class MFMs and other providers here to ensure that these deeply personal medical decisions are made between the patient and their provider at any point in pregnancy”, Dineen said.
Maternal-fetal specialists in Massachusetts played an important role in changing the law, Dineen said.
“That has been a real game-changer, having their expertise guiding the discussion again,” she said.
