articles.title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85
articles.summary:
Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile

Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled…

blocks.text: Patricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85. According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.

Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president. He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”

Born in Chile in 1941, Guzmán initially worked in advertising before studying film, first in Chile and then in Madrid. On his return to Chile, Guzmán responded to the febrile political atmosphere after Allende’s election in 1970, eventually completing the mammoth Battle of Chile documentary that chronicled Pinochet’s ultimately successful attempt to overthrow Allende, resulting in the latter’s suicide. Guzmán did not shrink from the brutality of the period, even including footage shot by camera operator Leonardo Henrichsen as he is shot dead by the soldier he is filming.

blocks.caption: A still from The Battle of Chile. Photograph: Collection Christophel/Alamy

blocks.text: Guzmán was helped in the endeavour by French film-maker Chris Marker, who supplied film stock and connections that proved vital to make the film. Guzmán himself was arrested but eventually released, but the film’s cinematographer Jorge Müller was not so lucky – along with his girlfriend Carmen Bueno, he was arrested, tortured and “disappeared” in 1974.

Guzmán completed The Battle of Chile outside the country, releasing each of its three parts – The Insurrection of the Bourgeoisie (1975), The Coup d’État (1976) and Popular Power (1979) – through the rest of the 70s. Described by the Guardian as “an outstandingly photographed example of a newsreel film that captures the drama and volatility of the period”, it has continued to attract acclaim since then. Guzmán revisited the film in the mid-90s with Chile, Obstinate Memory, in which he returned to the country after a quarter-century of exile. In 2001 he completed The Pinochet Case, after the Chilean former dictator was arrested in London in 1998.

The director moved on to more metaphysical subjects with a trilogy of films starting in 2010: Nostalgia for the Light, The Pearl Button and The Cordillera of Dreams. They sought to explore Chile’s traumatic past by absorbing the country’s magnificent natural landscapes. His final film, My Imaginary Country, was premiered in 2022 and covered Chile’s dramatic 2019 street protests.

articles.title: Kosovo’s former president jailed for 25 years over war crimes
articles.summary: Hashim Thaçi, 58, was convicted by The Hague for crimes committed while he was senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army

blocks.text: Hashim Thaçi, the former president of Kosovo, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison by a tribunal in The Hague for war crimes, including dozens of murders, committed during his time as a senior commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army during the country’s war for independence from Serbia in the late 1990s.

The European-backed Kosovo Specialist Chambers, convicted Thaci, 58, and three other former senior commanders of 96 murders, and counts of torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention directed at political opponents and civilians.

The convictions come at the end of a years-long process, strongly opposed by many in Kosovo, to bring accountability for crimes committed by KLA commanders during the 1998-99 war in which war crimes were committed by both sides.
Thaçi, who resigned from office nearly six years ago to face charges, stood in silence in The Hague as the presiding judge Charles Smith read out the sentence.

The former president, who served as the head of political directorate of the KLA’s general staff, faced multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity alongside the three other former leaders of the KLA who are widely regarded as national heroes in their homeland.
In addition to the murders, Thaçi was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people, torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of about 50.

blocks.caption: Crowds chant as people wait for the decision of The Kosovo Specialist Chambers on trial against leaders of former Kosovo Liberation Army. Photograph: Ferdi Limani/Getty Images

blocks.text: Once a hardliner, Thaçi shifted towards a more moderate political identity after being courted by western diplomats who suggested he could be a central figure in Kosovo’s post-war settlement.

At the heart of the prosecution’s case was the degree to which the convicted men had senior operational command over the KLA as a centrally-led armed force and whether the crimes amounted to a pattern of abuse.
The ⁠court ruled that Thaçi had “actively participated in and encouraged crimes”. Smith said: “The scale and nature of the crimes committed were very serious”.

He added: “The so-called ​intelligence on which many of these victims were arrested, detained and ‌killed was little more than unverified rumours. Based ‌on that information, victims were called and described as spies and collaborators and violently treated.”

Smith said Thaçi “used his position, leadership, authority and standing” to encourage crimes but insisted the trial was “not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army” or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia. Thaçi could appeal the verdict.

Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers court in The Hague had asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaçi and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi who had all denied the charges against them.
Krasniqi received 25 years in prison, Selimi 13 years and Veseli 18 years. Thaçi also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses that will begin this month.

The three-judge panel ⁠dismissed six charges of crimes against humanity and said prosecutors had failed to show these happened as part ​of widespread or systematic attacks against the civilian population ​as a whole.

Known by the nom de guerre of Commander Snake during the war, Thaçi stood out among the KLA leadership as an intelligent and articulate figure who would later charm diplomats – most notably the US secretary of state Madeleine Albright - at the negotiations in Rambouillet that ended the conflict.
But behind the self-assured image he projected as a senior political figure, he was long dogged by allegations of a darker and more ruthless side from his time as a wartime commander.

Thaçi’s defence partly rested on the notion that while serious abuses did occur, the KLA was a not a strictly centralised organisation, claiming that Thaçi’s senior position in the rebel group did not indicate culpability for crimes committed by local units.

“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaci told judges in February.

The trial was opposed by many in Kosovo. “A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision,” Kosovo foreign minister Glauk Konjufca told media outside the court.

Thaci’s PDK party called the verdict “a great injustice, because it is based on claims and materials that we consider fabricated and nurtured over the years by the state apparatus and Serbian propaganda to criminalise the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army.”

In Kosovo’s capital, Pristina, thousands of people watched the reading of the verdict live on a huge screen and were stunned at the sentence. Some started shouting “UCK,” the Albanian-language acronym for the KLA.

Thaci, who was born in Kosovo’s rugged Drenica mountains – the KLA heartland - was a philosophy student who rose through the KLA’s ranks, returning from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo’s struggle for independence.

Thaçi served in a series of senior political roles after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the The Hague. After the war, Thaçi became a central political figure and was instrumental in Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence.

Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of Nato airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.

articles.title: PDEA says P500-million confidential funds for anti-drugs ops
articles.summary: A member of the House of Representatives on Wednesday questioned the P500 million in confidential funds sought by the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) for 2027.

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 8:41pm

A member of the House of Representatives on Wednesday questioned the P500 million in confidential funds sought by the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) during the plenary interpellations for PDEA's proposed P4.4-billion budget for 2027.

In response to Philreca Party-list Representative Presley de Jesus' question about the proposed allocation, budget sponsor Representative Marcy Teodoro said the PDEA has been receiving P500 million in confidential funds since 2025, and that this was for anti-drug operations.

"High-impact operations and disruptions of major organizations. The NEP reports that in 2025, 1,471 of 1,991 drug-related information na reports are acted upon or 73.88% resulted in anti-drug operations. Admittedly, not 100% of the drug-related information are acted favorably," said Teodoro, who is also vice chairperson of the House Committee on Appropriations.
Teodoro, however, stated that the PDEA exceeded its target in going after drug suspects.

"In terms of percentage decrease in drug personalities, the target actually is 10% as set forth in this year’s budget. We were able to arrest 173 personalities totaling to or accounting for 10.18% of the target. So we exceeded a bit from the target," he said.

"In terms of high-value targets arrested, our target, as I have mentioned earlier, is 60% of the total arrests. And we were able to have an arrest of 2,368 out of 2,819 on the list. That is 84% accomplishment. And the number of high-impact operations conducted, as I have mentioned in my sponsorship speech, the 500 operations that we targeted this year, we already exceeded that in the number of 696 operations, as we speak now," he added.
Teodoro, who also sponsored the budget for the Dangerous Drugs Board for 2027 amounting to P526.54 million, also reported a decrease in the number of drug users in the country.
Teodoro, citing the 2023 National Household Survey, said that from 2019 when 1,675,000 individuals used illegal drugs, the number dropped to 1,479,000 in 2023.
"That decline is encouraging pero hindi ibig sabihin na puwede na tayong maging kampante. Mahigit isang milyong Pilipino pa rin yan," Teodoro emphasized.
(It doesn't mean we can become complacent. That's still more than one million Filipinos.)

"The task is broader than simply counting facilities. The value of DDB's coordinating role is to help government understand what kind if help is needed, where it is needed, and how people can actually reach it," he said.
The DDB is also responsible for coming out with the Philippine Anti Drugs Strategy (PADS) which is expected to be approved within the year.

"Kasulukuyan po, yung PADS natin ay nire-review. Nasa Presidential Management Staff ito for review and consideration at naghihintay tayo ng enhanced PADS based on the executive order dahil nagbago ang panahon at problema," Teodoro said.
(Currently, PADS is under review by the Presidential Management Staff and we are waiting for the enhanced PADS based on the executive order because the climate and the problems change.)

"Tulad ngayon, ang isang strategy pong kailangan ay hindi na ito dapat street-level drugs na lamang o kaya individual basis kundi ito ay naging transnational na yung [One important strategy is that it should not just be at the level of street-level drugs or in an individual bses, but on transnational shipments] shipment [of] drugs coming [from] outside of the country going into and being distributed. There's an observation that it's already a syndicate operating the drug distribution of illegal drugs. Somebody will finance it. And there will be in charge, different organizations and individuals, in the selling and distribution," he added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Party leaders to negotiate coalition in BARMM Parliament
articles.summary: Right now, 'it is the Bangsamoro Federalist Party as the single biggest party that will have the first opportunity to form a government,' says Member of Parliament-elect Ishak Mastura

blocks.text: ELECTIONS. Voters wait outside the precinct during the first parliamentary elections of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in Pahamuddin, Cotabato, on September 14, 2026.
Manman Dejeto/Reuters
Right now, 'it is the Bangsamoro Federalist Party as the single biggest party that will have the first opportunity to form a government,' says Member of Parliament-elect Ishak Mastura

items: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) is facing a hung parliament after the elections on September 14, with the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) holding 31 seats and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) holding 30 seats.
Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua emphasized the need for coalition-building among parties to establish a government, with discussions already initiated with other political groups.
The elected parliament will assume office on October 30, and a majority of at least 41 seats is required to influence the selection of the chief minister.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
COTABATO CITY, Philippines – After the historic polls on Monday, September 14, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) is now facing a hung parliament.
BARMM Interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua said a coalition with other parties is an “unavoidable situation” to establish a government.

“I’ve already called up the three governors, members of the [Bangsamoro Federalist Party], to come and discuss what we call the coalition or to establish a government,” Macacua told reporters on Tuesday, September 15.

Macacua is president of the leading regional political party Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP), which has a total of 31 seats. The United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), led by Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) Chairman Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim, got 30 seats.

“We need really to coalesce with parties that are likewise advocating similar platforms of government,” Mohagher Iqbal, MILF vice chairman and Bangsamoro Member of Parliament-elect, told media on Wednesday, September 16.

The Macacua-led BFP and Murad-led UBJP would have to establish alliances with the BARMM Grand Coalition (BGC), which managed to get a total of 15 seats, if their goal is to grab a greater hold of the Bangsamoro Parliament.

The BGC is composed of the Bangsamoro Peoples Party, Serbisyong Inklusibo-Alyansang Progresibo, and Al-Ittihad-Ungaya sa Kawagib Nu Bangsamoro. The coalition is led by Abdulrahman Rubbil Sangki Mangudadatu, alongside political dynasties such as the Adiong clan.

The elected parliament will assume office on October 30 and eventually choose Bangsamoro’s chief minister. A majority of at least 41 seats guarantees that the party with the highest number of members of parliament would have the most influence on who gets to take the seat as chief minister.
According to BGC nominee and Member of Parliament-elect Amir Mawallil, leadership in the coalition has yet to meet to discuss possible alliances with either the BFP or UBJP.
It is also possible that all three parties coalesce, depending on where the talks lead, said Ishak Mastura, Member of Parliament-elect for Maguindanao del Norte 5th District.
“But right now, it is the BFP as the single biggest party that will have the first opportunity to form a government,” Mastura told Rappler.

blocks.caption: Here are the results of 2026 BARMM parliamentary elections

blocks.text: Tensions among supporters of different parties diffused the next day, when results were being transmitted and winners proclaimed. Will tensions affect negotiations to form a government?

“I think the tension will eventually die down in due time,” Mastura said. “But right now, of course, people are still suffering from the pangs of the campaign. And it was a hard campaign. It was hard fought.”

Voter turnout for the polls was over 84%, according to the Commission on Elections. Authorities have said the elections have been generally peaceful and safe despite eruptions of violence in parts of the region. – Rappler.com

articles.title: First Thing: Houthis appear to target Mecca as House votes to end Trump’s war on Iran
articles.summary:
Vote comes amid Republican call to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth. Plus a catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn is returned home

Good morning. Saudi Arabia’s air defenses

blocks.text: Good morning. Saudi Arabia’s air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca yesterday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city. A spokesperson for the kingdom, which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen, said the security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”. Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest ​city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage.

Meanwhile, in Washington, the US House of Representatives has voted for a third time to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution a few hours after a Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report showed the conflict had cost at least $38bn and left the US stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild.

items: Why is Pete Hegseth being targeted by lawmakers? Republican congressman Thomas Massie has proposed impeaching Pete Hegseth, saying the defense secretary had repeatedly violated the constitution through his handling of war with Iran and the deaths of civilians in conflicts worldwide.

How is the Trump administration reversing decisions over arming Israel? Congress has been informally notified about a pending deal, with the US planning to deliver powerful 2,000lb bombs to Israel. The weapons prompted such concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration paused their delivery two years ago.

blocks.text: All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour of the US and Latin America have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opening act Macklemore, as backlash grows against his removal from the tour over onstage comments in support of Palestine.

Grammy-winning Macklemore had said on stage he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, along with the words “free Palestine”. The remark prompted a petition calling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour from the Israeli-American Council and the opposition of some venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and a prominent donor to Israel.

items: How has Ed Sheeran responded? In a lengthy Instagram post, the British singer said: “I have always used my platform and music to bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together … I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care. Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine.”

articles.summary: Rookie guard Kieffer Alas shows the way for Ateneo in its blowout of UE, which comes exactly 100 days since Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili died from drowning during the Blue Eagles' team building

blocks.text: ROOKIE. Kieffer Alas in action for the Ateneo Blue Eagles in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament.
UAAP
Rookie guard Kieffer Alas shows the way for Ateneo in its blowout of UE, which comes exactly 100 days since Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili died from drowning during the Blue Eagles' team building

items: The Ateneo Blue Eagles began the UAAP Season 89 with a dominant 101-74 victory over the UE Red Warriors, inspired by the memory of teammates Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili.
Rookie Kieffer Alas led the team with 24 points in his debut, while the team dedicated the game to the families of the deceased players present at the match.
Ateneo aims for a strong season after struggling in previous years, with assistant coach RJ Jazul noting the players' resilience despite their emotional challenges.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – With Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili in mind, the Ateneo Blue Eagles opened the new UAAP season with aplomb.
The Blue Eagles coasted to rousing 101-74 win over the UE Red Warriors to start their campaign in the Season 89 men’s basketball tournament at the Mall of Asia Arena on Wednesday, September 16.

Rookie Kieffer Alas turned in a UAAP seniors debut to remember, firing 24 points with 4 rebounds in just 20 minutes of action to show the way in the victory which came exactly 100 days since Baterbonia and Adili died from drowning during a team building in Dipaculao, Aurora, on June 8.
“I feel like this was just an introduction to Ateneo,” said Alas. “After everything that happened, everyone counted us out. So I hope that slowly, we can bring ourselves where we want to be.
Ateneo raced to a 25-16 lead at the end of the opening quarter and cruised the rest of the way as it leaned on the trio of Alas, Jared Bahay, and Grayson Rogers.

Bahay finished with 17 points, 2 rebounds, and 2 assists, while Rogers supplied 12 points, 2 assists, and 2 steals in the blowout which saw the Blue Eagles mount a lead as big as 38 points in the fourth period, 93-55.
It was a statement win for Ateneo, which drew inspiration from the presence of Adili’s parents, Elias and Ifeoma.
Elias and Ifeoma Adili are in the Philippines to watch Ateneo’s first two games of the season.

“The whole season, we dedicate it to Divine and Rene. But for this game, since you’re here, we dedicate it to you guys,” Bahay recalled from his conversation with the Adilis. “I made sure my teammates heard what I said so they know that we cannot lose because they’re there.”
Andrew Bongo also made his presence felt for the Blue Eagles with 9 points, 5 rebounds, and 2 blocks, Jay-M Leal chipped in 6 points and 9 rebounds, while Shawn Tuano added 6 points and 5 rebounds.

For Ateneo assistant coach RJ Jazul, the victory is a step in the right direction for the Blue Eagles, who are eyeing a return to the Final Four after failing to reach the semifinals in the last two seasons.
“The players’ emotional baggage will always be there, but still, they keep on grinding every day through hard practices. They’re all going hard,” said Jazul.

Toper Lagat finished with 15 points, while JM Edoukou put up 14 points, 8 rebounds, and 5 steals for the Red Warriors, who absorbed their 21st consecutive UAAP defeat, their losing streak dating back to Season 87. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Texas to execute man convicted in triple murder as a Georgia execution is put on hold
articles.summary:
Texas execution would be the fifth in the state in 2026, while Georgia has yet to put anyone to death this year

A man convicted in the shooting deaths of three people is set to be executed…

blocks.text: A man convicted in the shooting deaths of three people is set to be executed Wednesday in Texas. Meanwhile, another execution that was scheduled for the same time in Georgia has been halted by a judge.

This would be the fifth execution in Texas, while Georgia has yet to put anyone to death this year. The nation’s busiest death chamber is in Florida, which accounted for more than half the 25 executions already carried out in the US this year.

LeJames Norman, 40, was sentenced to death in the 2005 fatal shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, inside the home they shared in a small, rural town. He is scheduled to die by injection of the sedative pentobarbital at 6pm CDT at the state penitentiary in Huntsville.

Stacey Humphreys, 53, was convicted of malice murder and other crimes in the 2003 killings of 33-year-old Cyndi Williams and 21-year-old Lori Brown. He had been scheduled to die at 7pm EDT at the state prison near Jackson. A judge issued a stay of execution late Tuesday, but it’s possible that stay could be lifted in time for it to go forward.

Norman and Ker’Sean Ramey believed there was cocaine in the house in Edna, a small, rural city about 100 miles (161km) south-west of Houston, and hoped to steal it, according to court records. But they never found any drugs and fatally shot three people in the home. Lopez was shot four times, including three in the back of his head. Peacock was shot twice in the head. Roberts was shot five times to the chest, neck and head.
Norman was arrested about five months after the killings while trying to cross back into the US from Mexico. He pleaded guilty to capital murder, leaving a jury to decide his punishment.
Ramey was also convicted in the shootings and sentenced to death. His execution is set for next week.

The Texas board of pardons and paroles on Monday voted against commuting Norman’s sentence to a lesser penalty or recommending a 90-day reprieve of execution. After the Texas court of criminal appeals on Monday denied a motion from Norman’s attorneys for a stay of execution based on claims regarding actions by the prosecution, his attorneys have asked the US supreme court to review the decision.
In 2017, the supreme court refused to review Norman’s appeal raising questions about the competence of his trial attorneys.

The two women who Humphreys killed were working as real estate agents for a new subdivision in the Atlanta suburb of Powder Springs. He entered the sales office in a model home around midday on 3 November 2003, and forced them to strip naked and give him their bank pins before fatally shooting them, according to evidence presented at trial.

Humphreys withdrew more than $3,000 from the women’s bank accounts, according to court filings. He told police after his arrest that he had recently taken out some high-interest payday loans and needed money for a payment on his truck.

Witnesses told police they saw a man fitting Humphreys’ description at the sales office and a vehicle in the parking lot that matched his black Dodge Durango. Police zeroed in on Humphreys and tried to question him at his Dunwoody home days later. He fled and was arrested in Wisconsin after leading police on a high-speed chase.

A judge halted Humphreys’ execution late Tuesday after his lawyers filed a petition seeking a resentencing under a new state law that allows victims of abuse to have their sentences reconsidered and reduced if they can tie their crimes to abuse they suffered.

A lawyer for the state told the judge that if he ordered a stay they would immediately appeal in hopes of keeping the execution on track for Wednesday evening. The judge wrote that if an appellate court rules before the scheduled execution time on Wednesday that Humphreys is not entitled to a hearing on his petition for a reduced sentence, he will consider lifting the stay so the execution can proceed as scheduled.

Humphreys’ lawyers have also argued that he should be resentenced because his death sentence was tainted by a biased juror who lied during jury selection and bullied other jurors into voting for a death sentence. Courts have repeatedly rejected those arguments for procedural reasons, though US supreme court justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by the other two liberal justices, argued last year that the issue should be further explored rather than leaving it “caught in a web of procedural barriers”.

Additionally, Humphreys’ lawyers have argued that it was not fair that his clemency application was heard by only four members of the five-person state board of pardons and paroles. A judge had ordered one member of the board to recuse herself, agreeing with Humphreys’ legal team that there was a conflict of interest because she previously worked as a victim advocate with the Cobb county district attorney’s office and had worked with the victims in his case. The parole board on Tuesday denied clemency for Humphreys.

articles.title: ICC asks prosecutors to trim witnesses, evidence in Duterte trial
articles.summary: Judges question 193 hours of testimony and roughly 15,000 proposed evidence items.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — International Criminal Court judges have asked prosecutors to reduce the number of witnesses and identify the evidence they consider essential against former President Rodrigo Duterte — an attempt to narrow the case before his trial opens November 30.
Presiding Judge Joanna Korner of ICC Trial Chamber III said medical reports on the 81-year-old former president indicate the court will have to limit its sitting hours.
"It really is important, even more important than normal, that we conclude the case as quickly as possible," she said.
The status conference on Wednesday, September 16, was the third held since the case moved to trial, after sessions on May 27 and June 23.

Status conferences are hearings where the parties settle matters ahead of the trial proper. Today's conference dealt mostly with the prosecution's submitted list of witnesses, the hours it needs to present them, its list of evidence, disclosure to the defense and the incidents prosecutors want to add.

Duterte attended in person for the first time, having waived his appearance at the first two status conferences. His only previous appearance was by video link at his initial hearing on March 14, 2025.
Court unlikely to grant prosecution request for 193 hours of testimony
Prosecutors have asked for 193 hours to present their witnesses. Korner said that once cross-examination is added, that amounts to a "very lengthy period of time."

She did not rule on the request but told prosecutors to consider dropping witnesses, particularly as the list appears to include four experts on the same topic. If prosecutors send no proposals before the next status conference, she said, the chamber will go through the list "witness by witness."
"There are obviously going to be limitations on sitting hours as is clear from the medical reports," the ICC judge said.
"For the many reasons that I don't have to go into, we are very anxious that this [case] concludes as swiftly as his possible in the circumstances," Korner said.
Edward Jeremy, prosecution trial lawyer, said the list had already been cut and is still within the 175 to 200 hours prosecutors estimated before the first status conference.
Peter Haynes, Duterte's lead counsel, said he could not estimate how long cross-examinations would take until the court decides how far to restrict the prosecution.

He said the first prosecution witness is cited in only one footnote of the trial brief yet is scheduled for six hours of questioning. That testimony, he said, would begin in 1987, "thus embracing 40 years of Philippine history."
The prosecution replied that it would not be a 40-year history
Paolina Massidda, principal counsel of the ICC Office of Public Counsel for Victims, said the victims' lawyers "will probably not question all the witnesses.
She estimated they would need 30 minutes to an hour per witness. Witnesses to the crimes may take longer, she said, because the victims' lawyers would examine their victimization in more detail.
Court seeks 'non-negotiable' evidence
Korner said the chamber was "not prepared to agree" to the prosecution's list of about 15,000 items of evidence as it stands.
She reminded prosecutors of the court's earlier warning against the "wholesale dumping" of repetitive or barely relevant material.
"You don't have to put into a case every single document that has a connection to the incident. It's those that are most capable of proving what you wish to establish," she said.
Korner said she would order prosecutors to submit, seven days before the next status conference, a list of their key evidence: "the ones that are really absolutely non-negotiable in your case."
The prosecution said they would comply.
Nature of crimes against humanity case
The prosecution explained their list of evidence is a result of the nature of the case, which tries a former president for crimes against humanity.
In such a case, ICC senior trial lawyer and prosecutor Julian Nicholls said prosecutors must show not only that the killings happened but that they formed part of a broader attack on civilians.
"It's a crimes against humanity case where we have to prove the contextual elements," he said.

"There's a lot of evidence available in this case, more than in other cases I've done, partly because the accused was a president, the head of state, in a country where there was a lot of documentation generated," he added.
The prosecution also explained that part of the list comes from a single, large collection of government and Philippine National Police records on drug war operations in which suspects were killed.
He said the records give a baseline count of about 3,422 such deaths nationwide, and the files were "an absolute mess as we received it."
Prosecutors had also cast a wide net partly because the defense has not agreed to any facts, Nicholls explained.

"So far the agreement on agreed facts has been exactly zero. At this moment, we have to prove that he was mayor of Davao," Nicholls said. He added that the defense has not responded to 52 facts prosecutors sent in June for agreement.
"We may have gone broad. We'll try to narrow it down, but there were reasons for it," he said.
Defense laments 'unworkable' evidence load

Haynes said the prosecution's list is larger than the figure Korner cited. He counted 15,529 non-witness items and 3,712 witness-related items, nearly 20,000 in all, which he said was about four times the roughly 5,000 at the confirmation of charges.
He said 80% of the incriminating items arrived in the three weeks before the August 31 disclosure deadline.
"Realistically, that number of exhibits on the list is just unworkable," Haynes said.
"We haven't got a prayer of reading 20,000 items of evidence by a trial date that starts at the end of November," he said, noting that the defense trial brief is due Oct. 30.

Haynes said total disclosure has reached 62,500 items covering 324,000 pages, plus more than 1,000 video and audio files. He said prosecutors had held the police records collection since November 2021, but the defense learned of it only on July 15, six weeks before the disclosure deadline.
According to Haynes, no one had screened the collection for material that could help Duterte. He rejected the prosecution's offer to let the defense search it: "That's not our job."

Haynes also showed the court a four-page witness statement whose pages had been disclosed as separate exhibits, with page two never found. He said a 400-page document had also arrived page by page and the defense has only 347 of its pages.
He added that a photo of a strip light had been disclosed 21 times.
Korner told prosecutors the four-page example "is not something which inspires us with much confidence."
Haynes asked the court to move the case to a new case file and cap disclosure at about 10,000 documents.
"If I had a younger and healthier client, I would invite you to put back the trial date by six months and start disclosure again, but I don't. So, I'm looking for solutions," he said.
Nicholls said Haynes' account "is not all accurate" and "really exaggerated," though he acknowledged there may be duplicates.
Korner gave the defense until September 23 to file a written motion and gave prosecutors seven days to respond.
What's next

Korner said the chamber intends to sit continuously, from November 30 until the week before the Christmas break and then from January until the Easter break, instead of in blocks separated by breaks as the Registry proposed. She said no final decision has been made.
She also raised the problem of the time difference for witnesses testifying by video link from the Philippines, which will be seven hours ahead of The Hague when the trial starts.

Nicholls proposed starting hearings at 10 a.m., and possibly as early as 8 a.m. for video-link testimony. The expert panel had recommended an 11 a.m. start. Korner said the chamber was considering 10:30 a.m.
The chamber will rule in writing on pending motions, including the prosecution's bid to add incidents and whether Duterte should undergo further medical examinations.

The chamber has yet to rule on Duterte's fitness to stand trial. In a September 14 filing, Haynes said new examinations showed Duterte was suffering from significant memory impairment and asked for further tests by a neurologist.
Prosecutors have asked the chamber to declare Duterte fit and to keep him in detention.
In January, pre-trial judges had found him fit to take part in pre-trial proceedings.
On April 23, Pre-Trial Chamber I unanimously confirmed three counts of crimes against humanity against Duterte for murder and attempted murder allegedly committed between 2011 and 2019.

articles.title: Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
articles.summary: After Russia's recent drone attacks on targets close to the Ukraine-Poland border, Warsaw has doubled down on its support for Kyiv and pledged a "nonprovocative but serious response" to Moscow.

image.caption: A petrol station approximately 800 meters (874 yards) from the Polish-Ukrainian border was hit by a drone early on Sunday morningImage: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

blocks.text: Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland.

After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat.

"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday.
"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war.
Poland prepares response

Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.

"Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening.

blocks.caption: This truck was destroyed in a Russian drone attack near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn crossing on the Poland-Ukraine borderImage: Sylwester Uchanski/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe.
"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security.
Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train

Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.
Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.

Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.

"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."
Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down
"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.

Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.
Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland

Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.
But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.

In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up."
Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."

blocks.caption: Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that this is in the interest of Polish security Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added.
Polish media sound alarm
The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm.

"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."
"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote.
Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."

"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.

Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.
"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: ICC Trial Chamber rejects proposed setup for Duterte trial hearings
articles.summary: International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner on Wednesday said they are not inclined to adopt the arrangement proposed by the Registry to conduct blocks of…

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 8:00pm

International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner on Wednesday said they are not inclined to adopt the arrangement proposed by the Registry to conduct blocks of hearings with breaks and sitting hours in the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
“The Registry has taken the view that we’re going to have what has become, I’m afraid, ultra common in this court, sitting schedule then breaks,” she said during the third status conference.
“At the moment, we are not minded to do that. We are intending to sit through— we start on November 30th and then end, I think, it’s the middle of the week. Before the Christmas break,” she added.
Korner stressed the need for the trial to proceed as quickly as possible.
Duterte’s trial is scheduled to begin on November 30.
He is facing crimes against humanity charges over alleged killings during his time as President and Davao City mayor.
He attended his status conference for the first time. He was arrested in March 2025 at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport Terminal 3.
The former leader is currently detained at the ICC Detention Centre in Scheveningen in The Hague, The Netherlands.
He attended his status conference for the first time Wednesday.
Duterte sat behind his defense team. In the few moments that the former official was shown in the livestream, he appeared to be listening to the proceedings. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Microplastics in soil pose global threat by acting like ‘Trojan horse’ to deliver toxins
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Plastic surfaces form hotspots with an increase of antibiotic-resistant genes, study finds

Microplastics act like a “Trojan horse” delivering pollutants, pesticides and bacteria…

blocks.text: Microplastics act like a “Trojan horse” delivering pollutants, pesticides and bacteria through the soil, a five-year multinational research project has found.

The EU-funded project, which has so far resulted in 22 peer-reviewed studies, found microplastics in the soil of all 227 agricultural fields it tested across 11 European countries. The researchers said this poses a global threat, with healthy soils essential for life on Earth.
In many cases, this contamination reflected current farming practices as well as historical land use, demonstrating that plastic pollution can persist for many years.
The researchers also found that microplastics could interact with other agricultural stressors such as pesticides and veterinary drugs.
One study in Switzerland found that fields with the highest levels of tyre-wear particles also had the highest levels of other toxic chemicals and metals.

Microplastics can create new microbial habitats on their surfaces. Known as the plastisphere, these surfaces form a hotspot for interactions between plastics, microbes and agrochemicals, the researchers found.
An increase of antibiotic-resistant genes was found within plastispheres when compared with controls. Pesticides appeared to amplify this effect further.

Edoardo Puglisi, a partner of the project and professor of microbiology at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart in Piacenza, Italy, said the smaller the microplastics were, the more they tended to adsorb pollutants, microbes and DNA, leading to a “Trojan horse effect that can potentially increase the diffusion of pathogens and antibiotic-resistance genes”.
This Trojan horse effect can have an impact on earthworms and soil organisms by disrupting critical processes such as nutrient cycles, one study found.
Earthworms play a vital role in shaping the composition of the soil microbiome as well as the ecological functions of soils.

The research project also found microplastics could affect plant growth and function. One study found that higher concentrations of microplastics reduced leaf area, chlorophyll content, photosynthetic efficiency and plant biomass in lettuce.
When drought conditions were added, these effects became even more pronounced, with plants performing less well than under either stress alone.

Environmental assessments often consider pollutants individually, but the findings show pollutants can behave differently when they occur together. The researchers say policy needs to recognise that plastic contamination is part of a wider picture of soil degradation and pollution.

In an effort to reduce plastic pollution, there has been an increase in the use of biodegradable plastics. However, the project found biodegradable plastics were not automatically safer and could still degrade into microplastics, potentially causing ecological damage.

“Once these plastics fragment into the ground, they’re practically impossible to remove, acting as vectors for agrochemicals and altering critical soil ecosystems,” said Dr Esperanza Huerta Lwanga, a research associate in soil physics at Wageningen University in the Netherlands.

“To protect long-term food production and soil health, policy must catch up. We urgently need standardised plastic monitoring, full manufacturer transparency, and risk assessments that evaluate through different species how microplastics interact with co-pollutants.”

articles.title: Belarus to release 25 more prisoners as US eases sanctions
articles.summary: Belarus will release 25 more prisoners under an interim agreement with the United States, while Washington plans to lift sanctions on two Belarusian companies and pursue broader negotiations.

image.caption: Several prisoners from Belarus were also freed earlier this yearImage: BNS/IMAGO

blocks.text: Belarus will release 25 prisoners in exchange for a further easing of US sanctions, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday.

"We agreed on an interim agreement, and as a show of goodwill, Belarus will release 25 people. In exchange, the United States will lift sanctions on two companies," envoy John Coale told reporters in the Belarusian capital, Minsk.

Coale had reportedly requested the release of 250 prisoners during his visit last March. The US special envoy said both sides would work to resolve outstanding issues and secure the release of additional prisoners as well as the removal of further sanctions.
"We will continue to improve relations between the United States and Belarus and are working to secure the release of more people in the near future. We are not done!" he later posted on X.

Hundreds of people remain in prison in Belarus after President Alexander Lukashenko carried out a crackdown on protests against his reelection in 2020. Western countries then slapped sanctions on the country as a result of Lukashenko's repression of opposition.
Accusations against Lukashenko

Human rights organization Viasna, which is banned in Belarus, says the government still holds more than 900 political prisoners. The detainees have been accused of extremism, conspiracy to seize power, incitement of hatred, or insulting the president.

blocks.caption: Nobel Peace Prize winner Ales ​Bialiatski was released from Belarusian prison in late 2025 as part of a US-brokered dealImage: Petras Malukas/AFP

blocks.text: During Tuesday's talks with Coale, Lukashenko denied the existence of political prisoners and rejected Viasna's claims.

The two companies to be removed from the US sanctions list are Lakokraska, a manufacturer of industrial paints and coatings, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned company that oversees the forestry, pulp, and paper sectors. These sanctions have been in place since 2008 and 2023, respectively.
Coale also announced the release of tens of millions of dollars in frozen Belarusian assets currently held in US banks.

The Supreme Court (SC) responded to Vice President Sara Duterte’s remarks expressing distrust of the justice system, saying that it welcomed fair criticisms but needed evidence to act on.
In a 24 Oras report on Wednesday, SC spokesperson Camille Ting said that the decision-making of the courts was based on evidence.

“In my previous statement issued lately, we said naman the Court invites fair criticism as long as it’s… I mean we shouldn’t be very sensitive about the criticisms from the public, but then any action from the court will need evidence,” Ting said.

Duterte aired her frustration about the country’s justice system when sheposted bail at the Quezon City Hall of Justice for her three counts of grave threats against President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez.
“I do not feel safe, I really do not feel safe. I don’t trust the court, I don’t trust the police,” Duterte told her lawyers and surrounding reporters.
Duterte posted bail of P360,000 and was able to walk free afterwards. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi sentenced to 25 years for 1990s war crimes
articles.summary: A European Union-backed court on Wednesday convicted former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi of four counts of war crimes committed during his country's war for independence from Serbia and sentenced…

image.caption: Former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi appears before the Kosovo Tribunal in the Hague on April 3, 2023. Thaçi and three other defendants from the Kosovo Liberation Army received sentences on Wednesday. (Koen van Weel/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

A European Union-backed court on Wednesday convicted former Kosovo president Hashim Thaçi of four counts of war crimes committed during his country's war for independence from Serbia and sentenced him to 25 years in prison.
3 other ex-Kosovo Liberation Army leaders receive sentences of 13 to 25 years in prison

Thaçi resigned from office nearly six years ago to face the charges. He was convicted by a panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention.
Thaçi, 58, can appeal the sentence, as can prosecutors. He was on trial alongside three other former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders who fought Serb forces in the 1998-99 war.
Wearing a suit and tie, Thaçi stood in silence as presiding Judge Charles Smith read out the sentence.

The judgment was a crushing blow for a man once embraced by Western leaders, who invited him to 1999 peace talks in France, and who was seen as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.

The KLA leaders on trial are widely regarded as national heroes. In the capital, Pristina, thousands of people watched the reading of the verdict live on a huge screen and were stunned at the sentence. Some started shouting "UCK," the Albanian-language acronym for the Kosovo Liberation Army that Thaçi once led before entering politics.
One supporter, Bekim Fetahu, said the verdict was "a catastrophic decision."
"They [the judges] have put the victims together with the aggressors," Fetahu added.
Hundreds more Thaçi supporters were waiting outside the courthouse in The Hague.
Acquitted of crimes against humanity
Smith stressed that the trial was "not about the legitimacy of the Kosovo Liberation Army" or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia.
But the American judge said Thaçi "used his position, leadership, authority and standing" to encourage crimes.
The court ruled that Thaçi and his co-defendants targeted political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the KLA.

"In reality, there is no indication that the victims in this case were spies or collaborators," Smith said. Just having "Serbian friends or jobs in Serbian companies was enough to treat them as collaborators" of the enemy.

The four KLA members were all acquitted on six charges of crimes against humanity because the judges said the prosecutors failed to prove that crimes were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians.

As his trial ended in February, Thaçi told the judges: "Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo, defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice."
Prosecutors had asked for a maximum 45-year prison sentence for Thaçi and the other defendants, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi and Jakup Krasniqi.
According to prosecutors, the men targeted political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the KLA. All denied the charges against them.
Veseli was sentenced to 18 years, Selimi to 13 years and Krasniqi to 25 years in prison.
"This is a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our people and for our liberation war," said Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, condemning the verdicts.
Thousands of people had also rallied in Pristina over the weekend in support of the four men. The protesters filled a central square in the capital, many carrying red and black Albanian flags.

items: EU blasts Serbia, which wants to join the bloc, over 'shocking' funeral for war criminal Mladic

blocks.text: Portraits of the four former KLA fighters have been plastered across the city, along with a huge digital clock counting down to Wednesday's verdicts.
In Serbia, President Aleksandar Vucic said he planned to address the nation later Wednesday.
Separate trial on intimidation charges

The staff at the European Union-backed court are largely international due to fears about witness safety and security. In 2022, the court convicted two leaders of a Kosovo war veterans' association for intimidating witnesses by publicizing leaked confidential documents.
Thaçi also faces a separate trial on charges of intimidating witnesses that will begin later this month.

He was a student who returned from what he described as political exile in Switzerland to join Kosovo's struggle for independence. He earned the nickname "the Snake" for his ability to evade Serb forces during the conflict.
Thaçi rose to political power after the war but resigned as president to defend himself before the court in The Hague.

Most of the 13,000 people who died in the war in Kosovo were ethnic Albanians. A 78-day campaign of NATO airstrikes against Serbian forces ended the fighting. About one million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes.

In 2008, Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia, a move that Belgrade refuses to recognize. Ties between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense, despite years of negotiations mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

articles.title: Congo's Ebola epidemic may have gone undetected for months
articles.summary: The deadliest Ebola outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo may have begun months before it was first declared in May.

image.caption: As of September 12, Congolese authorities had recorded 7,200 cases in seven provinces with 3,475 deathsImage: Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Democratic Republic of Congo officially declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo variant on May 15. However, the first infections likely occurred much earlier.

Just how far back the start of the epidemic actually goes is still a matter of debate. But one thing is certain: Congolese authorities did not respond in the best possible way, with several international organizations highlighting delays in the initial response.
Congo is no stranger to crisis response. The country experiences Ebola outbreaks on a regular basis, and has in the past been praised for its expertise in combating the disease.
Early warnings came from WHO, Africa CDC

A good starting point for tracing the origins of the outbreak is the timeline provided by the World Health Organization (WHO) in collaboration with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak

According to their data, the first known case, identified retrospectively, was a health worker from Mongbwalu in northeastern Ituri Province. The person, sources said, developed symptoms characteristic of Ebola around April 24 or 25.
They died at a medical center in Bunia, the capital of Ituri. To date, 80% of all cases have been reported in the province.
It wasn't until May 5 that the WHO said it had been informed of "an unknown illness with high mortality reported in Mongbwalu Health Zone." The global health body then issued its first warning.
Congo's delayed response questioned as Ebola spread
Ten days later, on May 15, the Congolese government announced the Ebola outbreak.
Tests conducted by the National Institute for Biomedical Research in Kinshasa had confirmed the presence of the rare Bundibugyo type of Ebola.
Three days later, the Africa CDC raised concerns about the speed of Congo's response.
About three weeks had passed between the onset of the first symptoms in the suspected index case and the laboratory confirmation — even though the fatality was a health worker.

"This significant delay [...] highlights a critically low initial index of clinical suspicion among local healthcare providers, which facilitated wider geographic spread prior to the initiation of containment efforts," the Africa CDC concluded.
According to reports gathered by DW, residents of Mongbwalu had already reported suspicious deaths as early as the end of April.

"Several deaths were reported following high fevers, and the victims often showed traces of blood around various body orifices," said Dieudonne Lossa Dekhana, the provincial coordinator for civil society in Ituri.
Red Cross reported 'widespread' public fear 'since March 30'
There were other indications that Ebola was already circulating long before the emergence of this first confirmed case.

A May 16 report by the Red Cross of the Democratic Republic of the Congo stated: "Since March 30, 2026, there has been widespread fear among the population of the Mongbwalu Health Zone following a series of deaths."
Here, too, the symptoms matched those of Ebola: high fever, chest pain, severe exhaustion, persistent cough, nosebleeds, vomiting, loss of consciousness, a comatose state and ultimately death.

The Red Cross report said the trigger was believed to have been the body of a Mongbwalu resident "who died and was placed in a coffin purchased in Bunia, which was then replaced by another in Mongbwalu."
DR Congo: Ebola survivors fight misinformation
US researchers: February outbreak is plausible

The funeral that brought various people into direct contact with the body and the contaminated coffin is believed to have been the cause of a rising number of infections and deaths that were subsequently observed in Mongbwalu and Bunia.

But from the data available, it is not possible to confirm without doubt that these deaths were related to the Bundibugyo virus. However, they show that an unusual health phenomenon had already been observed more than six weeks before the outbreak was officially declared on May 15.
In addition, investigations since May 15 have come to support the thesis that Ebola might have been circulating even earlier than that.

In a study published in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on June 11, a team of researchers from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reconstructed the early course of the epidemic.

An initial transmission from an animal to a human, or spillover, between mid- and late February is "plausible," the researchers concluded. A late-April spillover, on the other hand, would be difficult to reconcile with the scale the epidemic had already reached at the time of the study.
WHO: Genome sequencing suggests February outbreak
On August 10, Mohamed Janabi, the WHO Regional Director for Africa, said genome sequencing analyses suggested the outbreak likely began "as early as February 2026."
Several early infections were mistakenly attributed to diseases that were far more common in the region, particularly malaria and typhus, he said.

In an August interview, Janabi told DW that there was a significant gap in case reporting. "The Ebola situation is catastrophic... In three months, we only had access to one-third of the patients," he said.

blocks.caption: Efforts to contain the virus have increased as the caseload risesImage: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/REUTERS

blocks.text: Could 'pig Ebola' shed some light on the matter?
Jules Villa, a researcher in the anthropology and ecology of disease emergence at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, points to a phenomenon observed in the connection with previous Ebola epidemics.
Villa'sstudy does not encompass the 2026 outbreak, but takes stock of local reports collected during earlier Ebola outbreaks in northeastern Congo.
Villa shows that livestock farmers, veterinarians and residents had reported unusually high animal mortality even before the outbreak of at least two Ebola epidemics in humans.
In 2017, several witnesses reported on what they called "pig Ebola" — a high mortality among pigs, which was ultimately attributed to swine fever.
According to Villa's research, monitoring livestock in the general population could provide the first useful warning signs long before an outbreak is confirmed by a laboratory.
Why is Trump investing $242 million in DRC Ebola response?
This article was originally written in French.

articles.title: Duterte team hits Prosecution's disclosure; prosec says defense is exaggerating
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team on Wednesday slammed the Prosecution"s disclosure of its evidence in the former official"s crimes against humanity case, saying that it is in a…

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team on Wednesday slammed the Prosecution’s disclosure of its evidence in the former official’s crimes against humanity case, saying that it is in a “terrible mess.”

During the third status conference before the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III, Duterte’s counsel, Peter Haynes, said that there are around 62,000 exhibits “dumped” in the Registry.

“Mr. Nicholls, I think unintentionally, has kind of muddied the waters here. Because the large disclosure package he referred to is not within that 19,000… nearly 20,000. That’s additional to that,” he said.

“And what has been dumped in the Registry is 62,500 exhibits. That 324,000 pages of evidence and over 1,000 video and audio files which run to many thousands of hours. And they’re in a terrible mess,” he added.
Haynes said evidence has been in the possession of the Prosecution since November 2021.
“That’s nearly five years. And the first time we knew about the large tranche was the 15th of July, six weeks before the end of disclosure,” he said.
According to Haynes, they looked into the possibility of acquiring an AI tool to review the documents.
However, he said it would cost nearly €500,000.
Haynes also argued that it was not their job to inspect the material.
“They’re supposed to triage this material and disclose it having read it. They’ve never read it. And they’ve had it for five years,” he said.

“As I say, I’m not going to go into the correspondence, but I have in front of me an email where we say, explicitly, we are not going to assume responsibility for inspecting and assessing the relevance of the documents in your possession,” he added.
Meanwhile, Haynes informed the Court that some documents were disclosed page by page.
He said a partial solution is a “meta data update,” but added that this only establishes the connection point between the pages.
“It doesn’t put them together in one document. There are still 400 separate exhibits,” he said.
Exaggeration
For his part, Prosecutor and Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said that what Haynes said was not entirely accurate and was “really exaggerated, in [his] view.”
“Yes, there may be some duplicates… I’m not saying it’s perfect, but that was not an accurate picture.
In response, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said that the example presented by Haynes did not “inspire them with much confidence.”
Earlier, Nicholls also said that he and the defense have yet to agree on facts.

“So far, the agreement on agreed facts has been exactly zero. At this moment, we have to prove that he was mayor of Davao. At this moment, we have to prove he was elected president and that he served as president,” he said.
Korner told the Prosecution to produce a list of key items of evidence.
Meanwhile, she directed the defense to submit into writing its complaints or suggestions within seven days.
She also gave the Prosecution seven days to give its reply.
Korner also advised the parties to discuss with each other.
Duterte, who is is facing charges over alleged killings during his time as President and Davao City mayor, attended his status conference for the first time.
He sat behind his defense team.
In the few moments that the former official was shown in the livestream, he appeared to be listening intently. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte defense considered AI amid massive ICC evidence review
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte's defense team said it considered using artificial intelligence (AI) and other electronic methods to review tens of thousands of documents related to his case, but…
articles.byline: JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III

blocks.text: Published September 16, 2026 7:11pm

THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Former president Rodrigo Duterte's defense team said it considered using artificial intelligence (AI) and other electronic methods to review tens of thousands of documents related to his case, but found that a suitable AI tool could cost nearly half a million euros (almost P36.18 million).

The issue came up during Wednesday's status conference before the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III as Duterte's counsel Peter Haynes raised concerns over the volume and organization of evidence disclosed by the prosecution.
Duterte appeared in person before the Court for the first time since his initial appearance hearing in March 2025.
Haynes said the prosecution's evidence list contains nearly 20,000 items, compared to about 5,000 at the confirmation stage.

"We haven't got a prayer of reading 20,000 items of evidence by a trial date that starts at the end of November, and even less a prayer of dealing with them in our brief, which has to be filed on the 30th of October," Haynes said.
He also told the Chamber that a separate disclosure package involved 62,500 items, around 324,000 pages of evidence and more than 1,000 audio and video files.
Trial Chamber III presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked whether the fact that the records are now digital and searchable could allow the defense to review them more quickly through electronic methods.

"Because it's all digitalized, it's more searchable. And provided you give it terms that meet the criteria, it is possible to go through it quicker than we're all in the proverbial boxes in a warehouse," the judge said.
Haynes said the defense had already researched the possibility of using AI.
"We did research the possibility of acquiring an AI tool to do it, and it will cost very nearly half a million euros," he said.

The defense also argued that prosecutors should have reviewed and sorted the materials before it was disclosed. Haynes said part of the material had been in the prosecution's possession since November 2021.
"They're supposed to triage this material and disclose it, having read it. They've never read it, and they've had it for five years," Haynes said.

Haynes described several problems with the disclosure, including individual pages of the same document being filed separately and assigned different evidence numbers. He said one 400-page document had been disclosed page by page, with the defense receiving 347 of the 400 pages.
He proposed moving a smaller set of materials to a new case file and limiting the disclosure there to around 10,000 documents.
'Really exaggerated'

The prosecution disputed Haynes' description of the disclosure. ICC Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said the defense's account was "not all accurate" and "really exaggerated," although he acknowledged that some duplicates and other problems may exist.
The Chamber said the issue should be resolved quickly and ordered the defense to put its concerns and proposed solution in writing.
"So, Mr. Haynes, we'll give you seven days. We'll say close business by next Wednesday to file a motion about this," the judge said.
The prosecution will then be given seven days to respond.
The judge also urged both sides to try to settle the disclosure issues between themselves, while acknowledging the difficulties involved "even with electronic methods."
"We obviously have to resolve this sooner rather than later," the judge said. — VDV, GMA News

His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.
Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".
Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.
He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.
"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.

Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.
He later became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.
His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.
In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.
In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

articles.title: Duterte makes first appearance before ICC judges
articles.summary: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the ICC as judges considered claims of memory impairment and poor health. The 81-year-old is accused of crimes against humanity.

image.caption: Lawyers for the 81-year-old have said he is suffering from cognitive declineImage: International Criminal Court/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Rodrigo Duterte, the former president of the Philippines, made his first in-person appearance before judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) at a pretrial hearing on Wednesday.
The 81-year-old faces charges of crimes against humanity in connection with hundreds of murders committed during his "war on drugs" while in office.
Duterte, who served as president from 2016 to 2022, denies the allegations.
He has missed a series of hearings since he was arrested in March 2025 and has previously appeared in court via videolink.
Duterte's legal team have said he suffers from poor health, but the court's judges ruled in January that he was fit enough to follow proceedings and requested his presence in court.
The ex-president "suffers from a significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing his memories," his lawyers said.
The prosecution, meanwhile, argued Duterte was "capable of meaningfully exercising his procedural and fair trial rights, and that he is fit for trial."
Philippines: Duterte 'must face reckoning' for drug war
What is Duterte accused of?
Rodrigo Duterte is accused of crimes against humanity committed between 2011 and 2019, first when he was the mayor of the southern city of Davao and then as Philippine president.
Prosecutors say he is responsible for a systematic campaign that led to the deaths of at least 30,000 people, many of them during "anti-drug" raids.
Duterte's trial is scheduled for November this year.
During Wednesday's pretrial hearing, judges were to hear arguments about his health and decide whether he is mentally fit to stand trial.
