articles.title: UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions
articles.summary:
Study challenges belief that temple’s curves were designed to correct optical illusions that would have ruined its clean lines

A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the…

blocks.text: A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens.

Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon’s clean lines.

But after a detailed investigation, and a flurry of mathematical modelling, Prof Alain Goriely at the University of Oxford has reached an awkward conclusion. The optical illusions the curves are meant to fix are either nonsense or practically imperceptible. In short, the illusions are themselves an illusion.

In his study, Goriely traces the myth back to the 1st-century Roman architect and engineer Vitruvius who wrote about the Parthenon 400 years after its construction. His account found its way into architectural books and became established fact. Today’s AI chatbots still churn out the tale. “I do think it might be the oldest myth that we have,” Goriely said, “apart from religion.”

A common claim that the mathematician challenges concerns the Parthenon’s base or stylobate. Measurements show the sides of the base are not horizontal but form a gentle arc that rises 6cm in the centre. According to Vitruvius, this corrects an illusion that would make the base appear to sag in the middle.
The sagging effect has been attributed to two proposed tricks of the light. The first states that long horizontal lines simply seem to slump in the middle, but Goriely found no evidence for this.

The second suggests that the Parthenon’s marble columns create the illusion. This is based on the Hering illusion where parallel lines on a 2D sheet can look bowed when other lines intersect them. But the Hering illusion is strongest when the intersecting lines are at acute angles. The columns at the Parthenon are too vertical to produce the illusion, and there is no proof it even works in 3D, Goriely said.

Another claim is that the bulges in the Parthenon’s columns – a curvature called entasis – corrects an optical illusion that would make them look too narrow in the middle. Again, Goriely found no evidence for the illusion. Moreover, the columns at the Parthenon bulge by a mere 18mm, which is barely perceptible at typical viewing distances.

Goriely, who assesses and dismisses other supposed “optical corrections” in his paper concedes he “fell into a bit of a rabbit hole” pulling all the evidence together. He suspects the Parthenon’s architects had other reasons for the architectural features.

The curve of the base may have prevented rain puddles forming and curved columns might simply have felt more organic and visually pleasing to the ancient Greeks, he writes in Royal Society Open Science.
It is unclear why the myth has endured for so long, but Goriely suspects that the perception of ancient Greece as a supremely knowledgeable and ingenious civilisation is partly to blame.

Unusually for an academic study, Goriely ends his paper by inviting readers to put it down and take a walk in a city. “Trust your own eyes, question what you see and decide for yourself whether the theory of optical corrections holds up,” he writes.

Frank Salmon, professor of the history of classical architecture at the University of Cambridge, said: “Some experts have long been cautious of Vitruvius’s explanations, recognising the risks inherent in using his text as a sort of bible to explain architectural practices in Greece centuries before his time, but also the loss of the many Greek texts about their temple architecture he claimed to have read when preparing his own.”

articles.title: 'Truth, fairness': Ex-CJ Panganiban questions fixed impeachment math
articles.summary: The ex-chief justice raises a point on whether senators who did not hear the case should help decide the verdict.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 11:18am
MANILA, Philippines — Retired Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban said the 16-vote threshold to convict Vice President Sara Duterte should not be treated as a fixed number.

Appearing before the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16 as an amicus curiae, or friend of the court, Panganiban said the constitutional requirement of "two-thirds of all the members of the Senate" translates to 16 of 24 senators only "in the abstract."
The calculation, he argued, "cannot always be reduced to abstract arithmetic."

Panganiban said senators should approach the constitutional provision with "common sense," guided by "truth and fairness," rather than rely exclusively on either a literal reading of the text or the intent of its framers.
He noted that senator-judges are not sitting as ordinary jurists but as elected representatives exercising the Senate's constitutional power to try impeachment cases.
Should absent senators vote?
Panganiban also questioned whether senators who have not participated in the proceedings should be allowed to cast a vote on Duterte's guilt or innocence.
He said determining the truth in an impeachment trial requires studying evidence and hearing witnesses in person, including observing their body language, tone of voice and spontaneity.
Fairness likewise requires hearing all sides before reaching judgment, he said, quoting the ancient Greek statesman Themistocles: "Strike me as you may, but hear me first."
Panganiban then raised the cases of senators who may be in hiding, abroad, detained, sick, hospitalized or otherwise absent from the proceedings.
Such senators, he said, would not have examined the documents presented to the court, heard the testimony or personally observed the witnesses.
"Meaningful adjudication requires active participation in this search for truth and fairness," Panganiban said.

In one of the sharpest parts of his presentation, he contrasted senators "sweating it out" inside the session hall with absent members who could be sightseeing by the Nile, shopping in Paris, riding gondolas in Venice or "deliberately hiding in the dark corners of the world."
He did not name any senator.

Panganiban's position adds another argument against automatically treating two-thirds of the Senate as a fixed 16 votes, although he did not, in the portions of his presentation summarized Wednesday morning, prescribe a specific alternative number.
Senate has final say
Panganiban also argued that the Senate itself has the final word on an impeachment verdict.
He said the Constitution provides no route for appealing a Senate judgment in an impeachment trial to the Supreme Court.

The high court may intervene only when the Senate commits grave abuse of discretion, he said, such as a capricious, whimsical or arbitrary exercise of judgment amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court cannot step in simply because it disagrees with the wisdom of the Senate's decision, Panganiban added.
The former chief justice is one of four retired Supreme Court justices tapped as amici curiae, or friends of the court, to advise senator-judges on the disputed voting threshold.

Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr., who submitted a written memorandum, separately argued that the two-thirds requirement should be based on senators legally and physically qualified to vote rather than automatically on the full 24-member Senate. — Based on reports from Cristina Chi and Martin Ramos

articles.title: For ex-CJ Davide, 16 votes not necessarily required to convict Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Retired Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr. argued that the two-thirds impeachment threshold should be based only on senators qualified and able to vote.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 10:48am

MANILA, Philippines — Retired chief justice Hilario Davide Jr. argued that the two-thirds threshold in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial should be based only on senators qualified and able to vote, rather than automatically on all 24 Senate seats.
Davide's position was contained in a memorandum submitted as amicus curiae, or friend of the court, which was read before the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, September 16.

He argued that senators facing legal or physical restraints that prevent them from participating in the trial should be excluded from the denominator used to determine the two-thirds vote required for conviction.

Davide, who was a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention and a member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission, said the framers did not specifically debate the meaning of "all the members of the Senate" in the impeachment provision.
But he said they understood "members" to mean senators capable of performing their duties.
Any other interpretation, Davide wrote, would "tolerate an absurdity, and perpetuate an injustice."
Under his interpretation, senators who have resigned or been expelled would not be counted.
He argued that the same should apply to senators unable to participate because of serious physical or mental incapacity, citing examples such as coma or terminal illness.
Davide also said senators who are outside the country, in hiding or whose whereabouts are unknown should be excluded from the count.

He further argued that senators under legal restraint should not form part of the voting body, including those detained while facing plunder or graft charges, those facing other criminal cases under circumstances preventing them from performing their duties, and those convicted and serving sentence.
Davide cited Supreme Court rulings holding that public officials in detention cannot exercise the functions of their office while detained.
'Avelino' case
Davide also addressed the 1949 Supreme Court ruling in *Avelino v. Cuenco*, which has figured in arguments over how the Senate should count its membership.
He said the case was not directly controlling because it dealt with quorum during an ordinary Senate session rather than the constitutionally required vote in an impeachment trial.
Davide nevertheless said the ruling had persuasive value.

In Avelino, two senators were absent, one confined in a hospital and another in the United States. Davide said this effectively left 22 senators capable of acting, making 12 the majority that elected Mariano Cuenco as Senate president.

Applying that reasoning to the impeachment court, Davide argued that senators who are detained, abroad, suspended or otherwise unable to take part in the proceedings should not be counted when determining the voting threshold.
The Senate impeachment court is considering an appeal of presiding officer Chiz Escudero's earlier ruling that 16 votes, or two-thirds of the full 24-member Senate, are required to convict Duterte.
Davide is one of four former Supreme Court justices tapped as amici curiae to advise the impeachment court on the constitutional question.

Retired Chief Justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno and retired Associate Justice Adolf Azcuna were also invited to give their views. Davide submitted a written memorandum instead of appearing personally. — Based on reports from Cristina Chi and Martin Ramos

articles.title: Lost on Mount Fuji off-season? You'll have to pay for your rescue
articles.summary: The fee will be imposed on those who get lost on Japan's most famous mountain during the off-peak seasons.

blocks.text: From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say.
The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers.
A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference.
Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans.

"We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday.
Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded.
Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas.
They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year.
Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations.
However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

articles.title: The Palestinian school under siege – podcast
articles.summary: At least five pupils at a village school in the West Bank have been killed in the last year by settlers and soldiers. Emma Graham-Harrison reports on how the school found itself…
articles.byline: Presented by Annie Kelly with Emma Graham-Harrison; produced by Ivor Manley and Brian McNamara; executive producer Homa Khaleeli

blocks.text: Waheed Abu Naim is an English teacher at the Al Mughayyir boys’ school in a village in the West Bank. He loves his job, he says. “I am happy to be a teacher. Although we don’t get lots of money, because my students, especially in the morning, wait for me when I enter the school to shake hands, to smile at me while going inside their classes. So it’s a happy life.”

But the last year has been anything but happy for Waheed. His village is now surrounded by settlers, while the military has blocked off every road except one, which has a checkpoint on it. Teachers who live in neighbouring villages cannot always come to work. But worse are the attacks on the village by settlers.
In April, a 14-year-old pupil was killed next to a playground gate after a gunman opened fire. As Waheed rushed the teenager to hospital he learned his own brother had also been killed.

Senior Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison tells Annie Kelly: “We’ve documented the hundreds of children who’ve been killed by Israeli soldiers, settlers over the last three years. But even in that context, of sort-of regular deadly violence, there is something particularly horrific about someone taking aim at a school full of children.”

Four other students were also killed and, says Emma, things don’t seem to be getting better. “In the next few months I’m just, very unfortunately, expecting to see at least the same level of violence and frankly, probably an escalation.”

articles.title: Saudi Arabia warns of ‘red line’ after Houthi drone intercepted close to holy city of Mecca
articles.summary:
The Iran-aligned militant group rejected the suggestion it had targeted Mecca, while the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned the attack

Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and…

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a ⁠Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, according to a ⁠spokesperson for the ⁠Saudi-led ​military coalition which is fighting the Iran-aligned group in Yemen.

The security of Islam’s two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a “red line”, ⁠coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the ⁠Houthis.

Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest ​city and the focal point ‌of the annual ‌hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims ‌undertake each year.
Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, after what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017.

A Houthi official rejected the claim on Wednesday, with spokesperson Hazem al-Assad writing on X: “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.”

The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned what they called a “heinous” attack on Islam’s holy city, blaming the Houthis. The group – which is made up of 57 Muslim-majority countries decried the “ongoing aggression against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.”

Saudi Arabia issued security alerts across parts of the country on Tuesday, including in Mecca and other ‌cities, following a week of attacks by Iran-aligned fighters that have drawn the kingdom deeper into the Middle East ​war.

The Houthis have seized control of parts of ⁠Yemen’s Red Sea coast overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, one of the ​world’s most important ​shipping straits, threatening Saudi oil ​exports rerouted from the strait of Hormuz.
The group has ​announced several major ‌attacks on ​Saudi Arabia over ​the past week, including strikes on an airbase on Monday that it said were retaliation for airstrikes on Yemen.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Remulla says Roque asylum bid denied; Roque disputes claim
articles.summary: Two contradicting claims, yet no proof bared just yet.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 8:47am
Former presidential spokesperson and congressman Harry Roque Jr. answers questions at the House of Representatives Quad Committee hearing on Aug. 23, 2024.
HREP

MANILA, Philippines (First published Sept. 15, 8 p.m.) — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Tuesday claimed that former presidential spokesperson Harry Roque's asylum bid in Austria had been denied, a claim Roque later disputed.
Remulla made the statement during a press conference on Tuesday, September 15, adding that authorities would move against Roque once an Interpol Red Notice is issued.
"By the way, na-deny 'yung asylum ni Harry Roque," Remulla said. "Kapag may Red Notice na, kukunin ko siya."
By the way, Harry Roque's asylum bid was denied... I'll get him once there is a Red Notice.)
Remulla did not disclose further details about the purported denial. Philstar.com has also reached out to the Department of Justice for more information but has yet to receive a response.
Roque, who faces qualified human trafficking charges in connection with the raided Lucky South 99 POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, has been staying in Austria while seeking asylum.
An Angeles City court issued a warrant for his arrest in May 2025 over the non-bailable trafficking charges.
Roque left the Philippines without a recorded departure in Bureau of Immigration records after authorities began looking for him in 2024.
The Department of Justice had earlier issued an immigration lookout bulletin against him and several others in August 2024 in connection with the investigation into the Porac POGO hub.
Aside from the trafficking case, Roque also faces a tax evasion complaint filed by the Bureau of Internal Revenue before the DOJ.
In an interview with One News' "Storycon," Roque denied Remulla's claim, calling it "fake news."
Roque said his asylum application had already been submitted for resolution and that he was still awaiting a decision from Austrian authorities.
"The truth of the matter is it's been submitted and we continue to await for the decision of the asylum office," Roque said.

articles.title: Ex-Duterte vlogger RJ Nieto gets Palace assistant secretary post
articles.summary: Former pro-Duterte vlogger Rey Joseph “RJ” Nieto, who was behind the now-unpublished Thinking Pinoy blog, has been appointed assistant secretary at the Office of the Cabinet Secretary.

blocks.text: September 16, 2026 | 8:46am
Blogger RJ Nieto, known as Thinking Pinoy, attends a Senate hearing on fake news on Oct. 4, 2017.
The Philippine STAR / Mong Pintolo

MANILA, Philippines — Former pro-Duterte vlogger Rey Joseph “RJ” Nieto, who was behind the now-unpublished Thinking Pinoy blog, has been appointed assistant secretary at the Office of the Cabinet Secretary.

In a letter dated Sept. 1, 2026, Marcos said Nieto may qualify and perform the duties of the office upon furnishing the Office of the President and the Civil Service Commission with copies of his oath of office.
Nieto confirmed his appointment in a Facebook post, where he shared his appointment letter and said he had yet to take his oath of office.
"There are still a few formalities to complete before I begin work," Nieto said.

He said Cabinet Secretary Benhur Abalos would decide his exact portfolio, adding that the Cabinet Secretary's office monitors whether government programs are being properly implemented and whether services are reaching the public.
Nieto said he is unlikely to work in communications, describing the position as not a spokesperson role.
"From what I understand, much of the work will be closer to my academic training. That suits me. Mahal ang Botox, kaya bawal ma-stress unnecessarily," he said.
Nieto became known for his Thinking Pinoy blog, which he started in 2015 and used to publish political commentary.
In October 2018, Nieto pleaded not guilty before the Pasay City Regional Trial Court Branch 111 to a libel complaint filed by then-Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV.
Trillanes accused Nieto of libel over a social media post claiming that then-US President Donald Trump had called Trillanes a “narco,” or drug lord.
Nieto was eventually acquitted in the case in June 2021.

In a separate case, blogger Jover Laurio, who ran Pinoy Ako Blog, filed a complaint against Nieto in 2018 over the publication of her personal information, including her full name, user credentials and law school.

The Makati Regional Trial Court Branch 132 later ruled in Laurio’s favor in the data privacy case. Nieto was ordered to pay P300,000 in damages and P50,000 in attorney’s fees and litigation expenses for violating the Data Privacy Act of 2012.
Nieto previously served as a part-time instructor at Bulacan State University and a columnist for Manila Bulletin.

He earned a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics with first-class honors from the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom in June 2026. He is also pursuing a part-time MSc in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Public Policy at University College London.

"I spent the past years studying mathematics in the University of Bristol. That training taught me to look carefully at evidence, systems and complex problems. Sana magamit ko iyon sa trabaho," Nieto said.
(I spent the past years studying mathematics in the University of Bristol. That training taught me to look carefully at evidence, systems and complex problems. I hope I can use that in my work.)
He also acknowledged that he still has much to learn, saying, “government is not a classroom.”
"Marami pa rin akong kailangang matutunan," he said.
(I still have a lot to learn.)

articles.title: Stephen Harper says Canada had 'no choice' but to walk away from U.S. trade talks
articles.summary: Former prime minister Stephen Harper, in his closing remarks at the Canada Investment Summit, backed the federal government's decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.

image.caption: Former prime minister Stephen Harper said in his remarks at the Canada Investment Summit that the state of Canada-U.S. relations is 'very sad, just as equally necessary.' (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
Former prime minister Stephen Harper, in his closing remarks at the Canada Investment Summit, backed the federal government's decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States.
Former prime minister backs Ottawa's decision leading to trade war with U.S.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper, who led Canada's Conservative Party for over a decade, backed the federal government's decision to walk away from trade talks with the United States "to see a trade war commence in earnest."
Harper delivered the closing keynote to hundreds of the world's wealthiest investors gathered in downtown Toronto for the first-of-its-kind Canada Investment Summit.
"This had to be a very difficult decision, but I do believe that our government had no choice but to take this path," Harper said.
Harper, who has described himself as "probably the most pro-American prime minister in Canadian history," acknowledged his own long-held admiration for our southern neighbours.
But Canada needs to remain committed to retaining its economic diversity, Harper argued, not allowing U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to "hollow out" the country's industrial capacity.

"It is clear that the current U.S. administration views our level of economic integration as incompatible with our separate sovereignty," Harper said. "Thus to maintain that sovereignty, we must pursue diminished reliance on the United States."
"I do find this all very sad, just as equally necessary."
FULL SPEECH | Harper backs Carney's decision to walk away from U.S. trade talks
Within Canada's departure from its previous relationship with the U.S., Harper said the country is discovering an opportunity to rediscover its true potential.
"Leadership is defined by taking accountability for what you can control," he said, and Canada cannot only blame external factors for the headwinds it faces.
Harper argued Canada needs to become "more internally competitive, more externally connected and more truly sovereign than it has been."
Harper's remarks formally wrapped the multi-day investment summit which was spearheaded by Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The summit brought together hundreds of business leaders, foreign investors and current and former politicians in the hopes of attracting $1 trillion worth of investments over the next five years to fund big projects across Canada.

items: Stephen Harper says Canada must urgently reduce its dependence on the U.S.
Harper calls for Liberals, Conservatives to come together in the face of Trump, separatist threats

blocks.text: Harper attended the summit as the chair of the Alberta Investment Management Corporation (AIMCo), a position he has held since 2024.

The former prime minister told the room of investors that Canada's resource development is its "competitive advantage," and said becoming an energy superpower is "critical to our prosperity and indeed to our survival as a country."
'I wish I had thought of it,' Harper says of summit
Harper faulted the Liberal government that followed his election loss in 2015, saying until that point, "Canada was poised to become that energy superpower."
He said Canada missed that potential "because of deliberate policy choices that followed over the next decade."
"But there is no point bemoaning what is passed," Harper continued. "Especially because the opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again."
Harper congratulated Carney's Liberal government on its efforts to fast-track major project approvals, in particular in Alberta's oilsands. He also commended Ottawa for holding the investment summit.
"It is such a great innovation that I wish I had thought of it," Harper said to a chuckling audience.
Amid the congratulations, Harper was clear: "More does need to be done."

He called for a removal of burdens and restrictions in Canada "that do not exist elsewhere," and for the government to reform its regulatory reviews and permitting processes to provide investors with a degree of certainty, "as we had set up a decade ago."

items: Carney government introduces mega-deduction tax measure to spur more investment
Canada's 4 largest airports to be opened up to private investment, Carney says

blocks.text: Harper warned that if the government doesn't clear those hurdles, the U.S. will continue to be Canada's sole customer and "they will not lack the urgency that we have lacked here in Canada."
"That is why I have to say that I am very encouraged by the detailed comments the prime minister made today on doing just some of these things, and I welcome them," Harper said.
"I believe that Canada's new government is committed to further reforms in these areas and committed to their urgency."
Harper's change of tune

Harper's closing keynote endorsing the summit and aspects of the current government's direction is especially notable given the former Conservative prime minister has not always appeared so onside with Carney.
Just last year, Harper accused Carney of inflating the role he played as Bank of Canada governor during the 2008 financial crisis, a crisis managed by Harper's government.
"I have listened, with increasing disbelief, to Mark Carney's attempts to take credit for things he had little or nothing to do with back then," Harper wrote in a fundraising letter at the time.

Carney was Bank of Canada governor between 2008 and 2013, serving under Finance Minister Jim Flaherty. Carney's campaign website stated that he "guided Canada through one of the most turbulent economic periods in modern history, protecting jobs and helping ensure that Canada came out stronger."
During the 2025 election, Harper endorsed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre "without hesitation, without equivocation, without a shadow of a doubt," for prime minister over Carney.

But over the past year, Harper returned to the limelight, delivering a number of speeches calling for Canadian unity and to reduce the country's dependence on an American neighbour that has become "hostile."

In February, Harper said Canada should consider tariffing U.S. goods because a one-sided tariff arrangement could decimate the manufacturing sector. Carney's government mounted counter measures including tariffs against the U.S. after trade talks fell through in August.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.

articles.title: What Carney's pitch for private investment could mean for major Canadian airports
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday he wants private investors to take over operations at Canada's four largest airports — in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver. Here's what to know.

image.caption: Melbourne Airport pictured in 2014. Australia Pacific Airports Corporation Limited, a private company, runs the airport under a 50-year lease from the Australian federal government. (David Gray/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday he wants private investors to take over operations at Canada's four largest airports — in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver. Here's what to know.
'This isn't going to be the situation where the concessionaire is allowed to just take over,' lawyer says
Canada seeking private investment for 4 large airports, Carney says
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday he wants private investors to take over operations at Canada's four largest airports, in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver.

Speaking at a government-led investment summit in Toronto, he said the policy change — which would maintain the federal government's ownership of airport land and assets — would allow Ottawa to shift spending on major airports' operating costs toward smaller regional airports. That, he said, could reduce traveller costs at those destinations.
Under the prime minister's proposed model, investors could manage airports for set lease periods, while regulation and oversight would remain with Transport Canada.
Here's what you need to know about the proposal.
How do airports operate now?

Under Canada's current airport operational structure, private, not-for-profit airport authorities lease airports from the federal government and run the facilities themselves, overseeing everything from runway maintenance and baggage handling to terminal building maintenance.
Airport authorities are financially independent and are responsible for setting their own fees and recovering their operating costs.
How could Carney's plan work?
Karen Hennessey, a partner in the business law group in Gowling WLG's Ottawa office, said Carney's plan likely would require legislative changes.

Hennessey said what the prime minister is proposing is a concession agreement, something similar to a lease. She said the government's expectations on service levels, performance, public safety, passenger costs and employee management would have to form part of that agreement.
"This isn't going to be the situation where the concessionaire is allowed to just take over and run it the way they would run any other business," she said.
Airport private investment makes sense now 'in different times,' Carney says
The concession holder, in turn, would want clarity on their investment commitments and the regulatory environment, Hennessey said.
"Like any commercial arrangement, there's going to be some balancing to be done to meet those competing interests," she said.
She said such deals could materialize within six to nine months if both sides are motivated. They could also take much longer to negotiate.
"Getting the structure right, I think, is more important than moving quickly," she said. "So I don't think we're going to see this happening in the short term."
Are private airports common?
Privately operated airports are rare in North America but not everywhere around the world.

A study published in the Journal of Air Traffic Management found 51 per cent of the top 100 busiest airports in 2018 had some type of private sector participation. Europe had the most private involvement at 43 per cent, followed by Asia and the Pacific region at 26 per cent.

items: Canada's 4 largest airports to be opened up to private investment, Carney says

blocks.text: Carney told the investment summit Tuesday that Canadian pension plans are already invested in airports abroad and he wants to bring that expertise home.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has been tracking the effects of privatization on Australia's airports, has said that passengers face price increases when airports become privatized local monopolies.
Its most recent report says while increased infrastructure spending will likely mean higher costs for passengers, people are generally satisfied with the services.

A 2023 University of Alberta study found privately operated airports tended to operate more smoothly, with fewer cancellations and more customer satisfaction with terminal amenities. The study noted this comes with increased fees — about $20 more per passenger.
What do Canadian airport authorities think about privatization?

Earlier this year, as talk of privatization swirled, the head of Toronto's Pearson airport said the existing public ownership model has served travellers well but she remained open to "enhancements" that tap into private-sector investment.

Deborah Flint, CEO of the Greater Toronto Airports Authority, said she shares the federal government’s goal of expanding Pearson’s capital value. She also said the current management structure has shown its worth by steering Canada’s biggest air travel hub through major expansions over the decades.
The Canadian Airports Council took a cautious approach to the privatization talk.

"Canada’s airports are always open to investment conversations that align with our growth and have affordability of air travel for Canadians at the forefront," said CEO Monette Pasher in an emailed statement.
She added that Ottawa had indicated it would "work with airports to … extend airport leases. Those conversations are underway."
What are opposition parties saying?
The NDP and Bloc Québécois both issued statements firmly opposing the prime minister's plan. Both parties said putting airport operations into private hands will mean increased costs for travellers.

"We should be making air travel more affordable, protecting good airport jobs and improving public infrastructure, not turning critical public assets into decades-long money printing machines for CEOs and their shareholders," NDP Leader Avi Lewis said in a media statement.

items: Private investment at airports will hurt workers and travellers, says labour group

blocks.text: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told a press conference in Vancouver he wants to see details of the policy before passing judgment.

"We want to make sure that it doesn't end up being sweetheart deals for corporate power brokers and Liberal insiders at the expense of hard-working Canadians who are already struggling to put food on their table," Poilievre said.
Where did previous attempts to privatize airports land?
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau's government launched a study on privatizing Canada's largest airports in cities like Toronto and Vancouver.
A 2016 review led by former cabinet minister David Emerson suggested the federal government could sell long-term leases for airports like Toronto Pearson to private investors in a bid to raise money.
The review found the high cost of running airports has made air travel more expensive for Canadians than for travellers in other countries.

In 2017, then-National Airlines Council of Canada CEO Massimo Bergamini called for a “clear repudiation of an idea that carries no demonstrable benefits for travellers, communities or Canada's airlines.”
The federal government opted against moving forward on reforms after receiving mixed feedback. It announced in 2018 it did not have plans to sell off Canadian airports.
With files from Alessia Passafiume, Christopher Reynolds and David Baxter

articles.title: Iran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report finds
articles.summary:
Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild

The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of…
articles.byline: Joseph Gedeon and Andrew Roth in Washington

blocks.text: The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found, in a damaging report less than two months before midterm elections where the war and the cost of living crisis will likely hurt Republicans at the polls.

The economic report comes one day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”.

The Pentagon’s report did not address an internal Pentagon investigation into the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people, including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying the results of the investigation that would show negligence by the Pentagon in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes.

The new $38bn estimate in the CBO report, which is some of the first public accounting of the cost of the war in Iran, was requested by the Democratic congressman Brendan Boyle, ranking member of the House budget committee. It also found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. And it estimated that the cost would grow $3bn for every additional month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation.

Much of that cost has come from missile defenses. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and Navy interceptors that CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”.

In a White House statement responding to reports of the shortage, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, separately dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true” in August.

According to the CBO report, the shortage would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains such an arsenal and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has.

Munitions have been the single largest driver of the Pentagon’s costs overall, CBO found: $21.7bn to replace weapons expended so far, of which $13.1bn went toward missile defense interceptors alone. The office also put a price on damage to American aircraft and equipment, including a destroyed Thaad radar system, and said it was forced to build its estimates largely from public reporting because the Pentagon did not respond to its requests for information.

The report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been.
It also said that the war had led to the “large expenditure of missile defense interceptors, which will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years”.

In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out (including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs), $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs CBO could not examine – a far larger share of secret funding than in past war supplementals.
CBO further added that it still cannot estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.

articles.title: Alberta NDP flies the anti-separatist flag to steal a UCP riding in Calgary
articles.summary: It's hard to find meaning in one byelection for a general election 12 months away. But the big referendum is only five weeks from now.

image.caption: Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi talks about his candidate's byelection victory on Tuesday, as MLA-elect Kyle Campbell looks on. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·Analysis
It's hard to find meaning in one byelection for a general election 12 months away. But the big referendum is only five weeks from now.
A surprise upset 5 weeks before referendum, and a whole year before next election
In among all the splashes of Alberta NDP orange and UCP blue, there was plenty of red adorning the front yards of many homes ahead of this week’s Calgary-Shaw byelection.
No, sorry, I’m not talking about Alberta Liberal Leader John Roggeveen and the 3.8 per cent vote share he snagged.
The red refers to the many Canadian flags homeowners have newly erected, and the pro-unity, anti-separatist lawn signs that have sprung up throughout Alberta.
The campaigning New Democrats sensed the kind of reception they’d get at those doors for their candidate Kyle Campbell, now the MLA-elect.

“If you were flying a Canadian flag or you had a forever Canadian sign … Yeah, we pretty much could mark you down as a supporter,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told reporters on Tuesday, the day after his party’s victory in what was previously a UCP riding in Calgary’s deep suburbs.
It’s often too easy and too foolish to treat the results of a single byelection as a predictor of a general election a year away, although darned if the partisans like Nenshi won’t try.
We’re likely on firmer ground trying to discern what a byelection says about the mood heading into the referendum about Alberta separation that’s set for five weeks from now.
Polls have consistently indicated that Albertans, especially in big cities, resoundingly support the “stay” option and oppose holding a future referendum for independence.

Now, another indication, in the form of voting results. At least in Calgary-Shaw, the public mood has turned against Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservatives, who thrust the province deeper into the unity debate by crafting and scheduling the Oct. 19 vote.

Shaw residents converted what was a 14-percentage-point UCP victory in the last election into a nearly four-point NDP byelection win. Of the 12 Calgary ridings that Smith’s party took in 2023, Shaw had the third-widest victory margin, a fact that might bring worry to UCP cabinet ministers and backbenchers in the city.

The win in Shaw was somewhat of a surprise to the NDP, judging by, among more publicly available factors, the fact Nenshi said his party’s relatively modest win margin “exceeded my wildest expectations.”

After all, the Opposition party had long been trailing the UCP in public opinion, and Nenshi lagged behind Smith, including in the city he formerly served as mayor. Most voters may have been squarely against separation or even the debate itself, but that dissatisfaction hadn’t been washing up on United Conservative shores. Not yet at least.

Smith and her Shaw candidate Mike Derry might have said repeatedly that they endorse staying in Canada, but Campbell and Nenshi spent much of the campaign trying to remind voters how responsible the UCP government is for the referendum — and that senior organizers in the party favour separation.

How thoroughly did the New Democrats wrap their campaign identity around federalism? After Campbell’s victory speech at a southwest Calgary bar, supporters spontaneously broke into a rendition of O Canada.
After the verdict that got his backers singing, a jubilant Nenshi called the byelection an “earthquake.”
“This means that 35 days from today, we send Danielle Smith and her separatist pals packing, and within a year from now, we give Albertans the NDP government they deserve,” he said.
Sure, Alberta would have a Premier Naheed Nenshi if Shaw’s 18-point swing from UCP to NDP gets translated to the rest of the province in the fall 2027 election.
In the same way that a stunner of a federal Conservative victory in a 2024 byelection in the Toronto riding of St. Paul’s led to Prime Minister Pierre Poilievre in 2025. Or didn’t.

In mid-2024, the Pierre Poilievre Conservatives stole a federal byelection in downtown Toronto, flipping a seat that had been Liberal for three decades. One year and one prime ministerial resignation later, the Liberals took the riding by 28 percentage points, and Mark Carney secured a fourth straight Liberal government term.
Ample time to interpret message

That Toronto byelection sent a political message of sorts that ultimately led to Justin Trudeau’s resignation. There’s ample time and opportunity for Alberta’s premier to interpret the message that voters sent her in the sort of suburban seat her party can’t afford to lose in a general election.

Barring another political “earthquake” on Oct. 19, independence referendums will be a distant memory come next fall. Alberta politics could change a lot before then; heavens knows they’re prone to turbulence.

Smith could pivot her agenda farther away from the independence question. She could give her Opposition less room to cast her as an agent of disunity, and themselves as the exclusive guardians of Alberta’s place within Canada.

It’s also possible United Conservative members give their federalist leader new marching orders on that same matter, and urge her at a November convention to get in line with many party activists and take a more pro-separatist stance.

The future could also be determined by what Calgary-Shaw and other ridings look like in the next election. Alberta’s electoral boundaries are getting revised by an unorthodox UCP-led advisory panel, with the prospect that the cities’ suburban ridings are spliced with more UCP-friendly rural areas.

The October referendum seems to have left its striking imprint in one riding. The boundary revisions will be but one of many factors that will colour in the map when all Albertans get to vote next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

Jacqui Lambie has warned Australians not to support a “dangerous” and “delusional” Pauline Hanson, drawing comparisons between the One Nation leader and controversial international leaders.

In a speech during adjournment last night in the Senate, the Tasmanian senator said she had received a stream of abuse after her impassioned defence of Andrew Hastie after he was repeatedly labelled a “traitor” in One Nation’s cartoon series.
Lambie said:

double quotation markOne Nation whips up the anger and they tell people who to blame. That’s the populist trick ... It’s a trick Australia, and we’ve got to wake up to it. Because every time a populist leader, like Trump or Farage, get any power, the lives of working people don’t get better. They get worse.
The outspoken senator criticised Donald Trump’s potential forever war with Iran while singling out Hanson’s support of his actions.
double quotation markYou’d put [Australian soldiers] back in another American forever war? [Hanson] is not only dangerous, she’s delusional!
Lambie said figures such as Trump and Nigel Farage were great at telling people they would fight for them while doing the opposite.

double quotation markSenator Hanson will be fine in her retirement, as will Nigel and Donald in theirs, because once again they are feathering their own nests ... Australia can choose not to follow the ugly politics of populism, we can do better because we bloody are better. And it’s not about right or left, it’s about respect and finding solutions, and not operating from a place of fear – whatever side you’re on.

blocks.text: Gambling company fined $1m for sending 800 messages to 165 people on Betstop

blocks.caption: Henry Belot

blocks.text: Henry Belot

Betting company Dabble has been fined more than $1m for continuing to send more than 800 messages to 165 gamblers who had joined the federal government’s self-exclusion register and asked to be left alone.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority also found the gambling company failed to close the betting accounts of 157 people who registered with Betstop, which helps people break their gambling addictions.
In a statement, ACMA said Dabble sent more than 2000 push notifications to 45 customers without including any information about the Betstop service, which is a legal requirement.
The watchdog has fined the company $1,069,200. According to Acma, Dabble has also given a court-enforceable undertaking to guarantee future compliance with the rules.
Acma member, Carolyn Lidgerwood, said the breachers were serious and undermined the federal government’s harm minimisation strategy.

double quotation markPeople who register with BetStop have made a clear decision to exclude themselves from online wagering. Providers must respect that decision by closing their accounts promptly and ensuring they are not targeted with gambling promotions. BetStop is an important consumer protection measure, but it only works if wagering companies follow the rules. The Acma will take action where wagering providers fail to meet their obligations.
Renters in NSW will be able to transfer their bond from one property to the next from today, meaning they won’t need to come up with thousands of dollars upfront every time they move.
It’s expected Smart Rental Bonds will save more than two million renters across the state up to $4,000 each time they move home – though the online scheme costs $25 to use.
The NSW government will pay the landlord the bond upon the end of the lease, while the renter will repay the government.
Renters will need to pay the difference if the second bond is higher – equally they will be refunded the difference if it is cheaper, provided there is no agreed claim on the bond.
The NSW government scheme has already seen $1m in bond transfers in Penrith, Parramatta and the Central Coast, where it was rolled out early.

It follows similar moves to make renting fairer in NSW, including a ban on no grounds evictions, a limit of one rent increase a year, enforcing fee-free ways to pay rent and making it easier for people to have pets.
NSW One Nation leader fronts rally opposing 'abortion to birth'

blocks.caption: Caitlin Cassidy

blocks.text: Caitlin Cassidy

The head of One Nation in New South Wales has fronted a rally opposing “abortion up to birth” ahead of an expected vote in the upper house on Libertarian member John Ruddick’s bill to ban “sex-selective abortions” during private member’s business today.

Mike Newman appeared alongside members of fringe parties outside the state’s parliament house on Tuesday evening, where he claimed One Nation wanted to “stop” abortion rights. Stumbling upon his words, he told the crowd:

double quotation markWe want to stop it. We want to make sure that same-sex-, sorry, abortion is stopped. We want to make sure that people have the right to life, and we will vote for you in favour of that.

Debate on Ruddick’s bill was adjourned in the June sitting week, and is expected to be decided via a conscience vote. Labor and opposition sources said the vote was expected to be close, or for support for Ruddick’s bill to fall slightly short.
The event follows another anti-abortion rally in June, attended by One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce, where he piled pressure on Nationals MPs to vote on favour of the bill.

Some members were expected to be absent for today’s vote, including Shooters, Farmers and Fishers MLC Robert Borsak, who spoke in favour of the bill in June. A senior Liberal source said that without members including Borsak, there did not appear to be “any room or margin” which could deliver Ruddick’s bill.

Richard Marles was also asked about Aukus, and whether he was concerned about reports from the UK which indicated the Labour government was delaying its decision about begginning building the boats by two years to 2028.
He said there was “no change” on Australia’s end in terms of the UK’s position and rejected that they were “red flags”.

double quotation markThe ultimate number of submarines is not the key issue here, the key issue is the development of the design, the pace of that which is happening. The UK is on track to cut steel in respect of its first SSN Aukus submarine next year. It’s on track to have that submarine come off the production line in the UK in the late 2030s. That’s perfect timing in respect of what we’re doing … We are really comfortable with what is happening there.

The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, says he is “comforted” by a recent essay from the boss of artificial intelligence company Anthropic which warned his industry must slow the pace in developing AI systems.
Appearing on ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening, Marles was asked about Dario Amodei’s comments urging governments to press pause on the AI revolution.
He replied:

double quotation markI actually take comfort in Dario Amodei’s essay and the call he’s made … It’s firstly not about … stopping this all together but rather making sure that the development of the safeguards that are in place in respect of this technology is in front of the technological capability itself … The technology is being developed very quickly, and … from an Australian point of view, our focus is making sure that in seeing this as a revolutionary technology which can be doing so much good in Australia that, we do have in place … AI safeguards in Australia which make sure that this is a technology which is benefit Australians and not the other way around.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.
Jacqui Lambie has launched a fiery attack on Pauline Hanson, urging Australians not to support the “dangerous” and “delusional” One Nation leader. More coming up.

articles.title: Turkey's rights groups, EU call out LGBTQ+ crackdown
articles.summary: Several raids and arrests of LGBTQ+ persons in Turkey have triggered sharp criticism from numerous Turkish organizations — and also from Brussels.

image.caption: Police raids in Turkey targeted the LGBTQ+ community (File from Istanbul's Pride march in June 2022)Image: Kemal Aslan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: During weekend raids targeting LGBTQ+ activists and organizations in Turkey, several people were arrested and many social media accounts were blocked. The Turkish government's actions have drawn sharp criticism from across the country and abroad.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had announced the operation as part of the "Decade of Family and Population" scheme, a national strategy proclaimed in May 2025 that was to counter the drastic decline in the country's birth rate and strengthen the traditional, conservative family view.
Istanbul saw renewed demonstrations on Tuesday, with LGBTQ+ associations emphasizing in a joint declaration that it wasn't a crime to set up an association and advocate for rights.
"Freedom of assembly, freedom of opinion, protection of privacy and presumption of innocence apply to LGBTQ+ people as well," the declaration stated.

blocks.caption: More than 100 women's rights groups signed a joint declaration in which they criticized authoritarianism in TurkeyImage: Murat Kocabas/AFP

blocks.text: The LGBTQ+ community also received support from the women's movement, with 120 women's rights organizations signing a joint declaration in which they criticized authoritarianism in Turkey.

"As women, we stand against the operations carried out in the name of 'keeping the family safe.' We know that the repression of our bodies, our lives, our identities and our right to organize is part of the same authoritarian politics. Being [LGBTQ+] is not a crime! Organizing as [LGBTQ+] people is not a crime!"
Government aims to 'criminalize' LGBTQ+ community

The government is trying to criminalize the LGBTQ+ community, said Yildiz Taghizade, advocacy officer at Women for Women's Human Rights (WWHR), an organization that co-signed the declaration. This criminalization did not just start with the operations of the past few days, but had already been going on for a few years, according to Taghizade.

"The aim is not only to target LGBTQ+ people, but to practically ban the LGBTQ+ community from engaging in politics, getting organized, claiming rights and showing presence in the public sphere," Taghizade said.
It was no coincidence that the operation came with the slogan "My family is safe."

"The government is trying to justify its actions by invoking the protection of families and children, but this narrative doesn't work. Because when we look at Turkey today and what is actually a factor of uncertainty for families, we come across very concrete issues such as poverty, the housing crisis, unemployment, care work [caring for and tending to relatives — Editor's note] passed on to women, and male violence against women," Taghizade said.

blocks.caption: In the western city of Izmir on Sunday, Turkish police fired tear gas at demonstratorsImage: Murat Kocabas/AFP

blocks.text: Criticism from medical community, trade associations, politicians

Other organizations have also criticized the government's actions. The Turkish Medical Association described them as a violation of human rights, demanding an end to the politics of discrimination. It was unacceptable, it said, to treat gender identity and sexual orientation as a crime, take people out of their homes at night and block digital channels — all in the name of family protection and security.
Erkan Bas, head of the Turkish Workers' Party, called for the immediate release of those arrested, arguing that the mere existence of LGBTQ+ persons was no crime.

But all those who did not share the government's views were "'called to order' by judiciary, truncheon and censorship. If they had their way, they'd love nothing more than to enshrine the criminal offense of 'being an opponent of the government' by law and sit back," said Bas.
Social media accounts blocked over 'national security'

The raids took place on Sunday in Istanbul, Ankara and Izmir. Over the weekend, numerous websites and social media accounts belonging to LGBTQ+ groups, various organizations and activists were blocked. On the day of the raids, another 32 accounts were suspended. The next day, the number of blocked accounts reached a total of more than 100.

Among those affected were Amnesty International Turkey, the left-leaning Evrensel newspaper, the Academics for Peace initiative, the Lawyers for Justice association, the women's rights organization Mor Dayanisma, the LGBTQ+ rights group Kaos GL and the Media and Law Studies Association.

The legal basis was a ruling by an Istanbul court announced on September 13. The Public Prosecutor's Office in Bakirkoy justified the suspensions by citing investigations into accounts that had spread "obscene content and LGBTQ+ propaganda."
According to several media outlets, the accounts were also blocked on grounds of "national security." Critics called the move digital censorship.
Queer life under Erdogan
Homosexuality not a criminal offense
Homosexual relationships are not a criminal offense in Turkey. However, the Turkish government has repeatedly referred to the LGBTQ+ community as a movement of "perverts."

Justice Minister Akin Gurlek has accused LGBTQ+ organizations of "promoting immorality," and declared on social media that "no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated."
'Stigmatization and discrimination' against EU's values
The European Union has also expressed concern over the weekend crackdown.

Commission Spokesperson Christian Wigand pointed out that Turkey, as an EU accession candidate, "should promote and ensure respect for the human rights and dignity of all individuals, irrespective of their gender identity or sexual orientation." He added that "stigmatization and discrimination are contrary to the values of the union."
Emma Sinclair-Webb, Turkey director at Human Rights Watch, interpreted the arrests as proof of the government's intention to criminalize LGBTQ+ persons without enacting new laws.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election
articles.summary:
Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates

Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.

The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.

During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”
“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.
Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.

“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”

The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pits Moraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.

Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.

Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.

With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.

The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.

Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.

Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.

Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealed an explosive police dossier relating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. In one text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”

Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.

The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.

The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.

“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.
Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.

Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.
In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.

“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.
“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.

articles.title: Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat
articles.summary:
Prime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment Summit

Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic…
articles.byline: Leyland Cecco in Toronto and Jennifer Rankin in Strasbourg

blocks.text: Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”.

Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States.
Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation.

“The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies.

“Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”

While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country.

That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks.

Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels.

European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy.

Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence.

“Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.”

The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe.

But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force.

French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.”

Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain.
EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 when Ceta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn.

Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner.

“We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”
In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US.

Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.”

Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted.

Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed.
But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some.

Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for the Many vs the Money counter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects.

“Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.”
Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s office announced nearly C$500bn in new domestic investment.

“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”
