articles.title: South African president vows justice as more women's bodies found near Johannesburg
articles.summary: Police have not linked the deaths to a serial killer but are investigating this possibility.

blocks.text: South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" in finding those behind the killings of several women in and around the town of Kempton Park, north-east of Johannesburg, over the last two months.
Another body was discovered on Tuesday morning and police say their investigation now includes the deaths of seven women most of whom have been found either partially or fully naked.
"These incidents are causing fear and uncertainty in our communities, and especially among women," the president said.
Police say they are not linking the deaths to a serial killer at this stage, but are investigating the possibility that a group of people is behind the killings.
"[It] could be that it's a copycat crime that is happening right here but so far, no linkages as yet," police spokesperson Brig Athlenda Mathe said.
One arrest has been made in connection with the discovery of the first body. The person is still in police custody.
So far only two of the seven women have been identified.
On Monday, police said that one of them was Elizabeth Moselakgomo, a runner whose disappearance last week sparked a frantic and public search for her.

President Ramaphosa said he had directed that the cases be prioritised: "Our law enforcement agencies are working urgently to establish the facts, keep communities safe and bring the perpetrator or perpetrators to justice."
South Africa experiences some of the world's highest levels of gender-based violence (GBV), with the rate at which women are killed five times higher than the global average, according to UN Women.
The discoveries of the bodies have sparked outrage and fear across the country, with many criticising the authorities for failing to adequately protect women.

Moselakgomo was identified by her relatives on Monday after her body was discovered on Saturday. It was the 38-year-old's young daughter who raised the alarm about her disappearance after she failed to return from her daily run last Wednesday.
The body of the first woman was found in mid-July, the second in late August - the others were discovered this month, two in the last two days.
On Tuesday, police said that the body of woman found on 7 September in a town nearby Kempton Park was also being included - bringing the total number of bodies being investigated to seven.

"After noticing that there are bodies being picked up, we went back to our police stations… and unfortunately it came to light that a body of a female in her late 20s was observed in a river next to a mall," Maj-Gen Fred Kekana, acting police chief for Gauteng province, said at a briefing.
Police have urged women in the Kempton Park area - which is by South Africa's main international airport - to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".
South Africa's Commission for Gender Equality urged residents of Kempton Park to work with the police to find the perpetrators.
"These deaths are indicative that women in South Africa continue to face environments in which their ordinary freedom of movement can become a matter of life and death," it said.

"Women should be able to run, walk to work, use public transport, return home, visit friends and participate in community life without having to calculate whether an ordinary activity could place their lives at risk."

articles.title: Drivers in Germany fume over soaring fuel prices
articles.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz wants to provide relief to motorists. But exactly how this is to happen remains unclear.

image.caption: In Germany, a liter of fuel now costs about three euros — that is more than €11 ($12.70) for a gallonImage: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gas stations in Germany are only allowed to raise their fuel prices once a day, at 12 noon. In Berlin, on the morning of September 15, E10 gasoline cost about €2.25 ($2.60) per liter and diesel about €2.37. At noon, prices rose by about €0.20 per liter. The highest prices were recorded at a highway gas station in southern Berlin, where Super Plus cost €3.03 per liter.

Drivers are angry. While it's possible to use public transportation in large cities, residents of rural areas have hardly any realistic alternative to driving. Those living in regions near national borders have an advantage.

On September 7, filling up a 60-liter tank with E10 gasoline cost about €31 less in the Czech Republic and Poland than in Germany. In Luxembourg, the difference was €28, and in Austria, €25. These figures were calculated by the Federal Statistical Office.

Germany has nine neighboring countries. Gasoline is significantly cheaper in seven of them, and diesel is cheaper in six. Only in the Netherlands and Denmark do drivers have to pay more for fuel than in Germany.
German government expresses 'great and growing' concern
But relief is in sight. That's what Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) has promised.

"Many people who need their cars every day have reached their breaking point," Merz said Tuesday at an event hosted by the German Foreign Trade Association (BGA) in Berlin. "I believe we must take action."
However, the chancellor added that the "exact measures" have not yet been determined.
"We are therefore in close dialogue within the federal government and with the German states." A proposal will be announced "very soon," Merz said.
But what might that look like? On Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin, deputy government spokesperson Steffen Meyer rejected any government responsibility for the high prices.

"It's not the actions of the federal government or anything like that causing prices to rise so sharply. Rather, it's largely due to the escalating situation in the Middle East, attacks on oil pipelines and the blockade of shipping lanes," Meyer said.

The fact is, however, that Germany imposes higher taxes and levies on fuels. The ADAC automobile club has pointed out that while the oil price remains below previous peaks, E10 gasoline is more expensive than ever before.
"From the ADAC's perspective, there is therefore a need to provide greater clarity, especially regarding refinery and wholesale markets," said an ADAC spokeswoman.
Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices
Price gouging at the pumps
Herbert Rabl of the Gas Station Interest Group (TIV) puts it more bluntly.
"They're raking it in. The oil companies aren't cutting into their profit margins at all," Rabl told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
He said that this is an issue that has long been the subject of political debate, but that the federal government remains divided on what, if anything, can be done about it.

However, the problem that the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) face as coalition partners is that the state coffers are empty, and the federal government cannot cover its budget shortfall without taking on a historically high level of new debt.
"Ultimately, the only way to bring these prices down is to end the hostilities and ensure the freedom of navigation," said spokesperson Meyer.
A new fuel rebate or tax relief?

Faced with rising oil prices that followed the outbreak of the war on Iran, the German government introduced a fuel rebate in the spring. From May 1 through June 30, 2026, the energy tax on gasoline and diesel was temporarily reduced. Factoring in value-added tax, this was expected to lower fuel prices by about €0.17 per liter.
"We had a fuel rebate; we subsidized prices," Federal Economy Minister Katherina Reiche (CDU) told the n-tv network.
But she says that won't be possible again: "Together, we in the coalition have decided that we don't have the financial scope for that at the moment."
As an alternative, the Conservatives are exploring the possibility of at least providing tax relief for commuters or supporting low-income earners with direct payments.

But that's not enough for the SPD. It is proposing a completely different approach and, as it did shortly after the outbreak of the Iran war, is advocating for a government-imposed cap on fuel prices. One of the ways they plan to finance this relief is through an excess profit tax on energy companies. In addition, the SPD supports a temporary reduction in energy taxes to deal with crises. Their goal is an immediate price reduction at the gas pump.
Saudi oil pipeline attack could raise global gas prices
AfD standing to profit from bickering

But while the federal government continues to debate and weigh its options amid internal disagreements, other parties feel time is running out. Regional elections will be held in two states on September 20.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, SPD Premier Manuela Schwesig is fighting to stave off a win for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). In the latest polls, the AfD was in the lead with 38%, while the SPD has recently gained ground, and is now polling at 34%.

The AfD wants to drastically lower fuel prices by abolishing the CO₂ tax on fossil fuels and reducing the energy tax to the European minimum. It also proposes lowering the German value-added tax on gasoline and diesel from 19% to 7%.
"There is the option of introducing a fuel cap and, at the same time, an excess profit tax, as in Luxembourg," Schwesig said on Monday (Sept. 14) in Schwerin.
She criticized the federal government's inaction: "The chancellor is just allowing this to drag on, and that is causing frustration."
A solution from the EU?

According to the SPD-led Federal Finance Ministry, Minister Lars Klingbeil will "strongly push" for the introduction of an excess profits tax at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin this coming Friday.
Officials in Berlin point out that an excess profits tax is currently being discussed at the European level.
"Large member states such as Spain and Poland are on our side," said a spokesperson for the Finance Ministry on Monday (Sept. 14) in Berlin.

"Such an excess profits tax would be one way to use the excessive profits that oil companies are reaping during this crisis — by fleecing consumers and imposing excessive price hikes — to provide targeted relief for the people who are particularly affected by these high gas prices," he added.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Holocaust survivor on 'very dangerous' AfD Saxony-Anhalt win
articles.summary: Charlotte Knobloch survived the Holocaust by passing as the daughter of non-Jewish farmers. She recently spoke with DW to express her shock following the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt's state election.

image.caption: Charlotte Knobloch is appalled by the AfD's election victory in Saxony-AnhaltImage: DW

blocks.text: Charlotte Knobloch, president of the Jewish Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria, is dismayed by the electoral victory of the nationalist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Knobloch told DW that there were now once again a number of Jewish people who, in the wake of such events, were considering leaving Germany.
It took decades, Knobloch said, for Jews in Germany to regain trust in the country after the Holocaust. That had ultimately been achieved. But now, fear has returned.

"That is, in sum, the biggest problem for me, because we successfully tried to rebuild the Jewish communities after 1945, to give the Jewish people a home again, which they hadn't had for a long time," she said.

blocks.caption: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund's (center) party received nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-AnhaltImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Standing up against the far right 'requires some courage'

In Saxony-Anhalt's September 6 state election, the AfD, classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the state's Office for the Protection of the Constitution, received almost 44% of the vote. Although AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund fell short of an absolute majority, he still has a good chance of becoming the next premier in the state parliament, meaning he'd become the first head of a state government from a right-wing extremist party after World War II.

"We can't allow any of those people to become state premier," said Knobloch. "It is a very dangerous situation at the moment, in my view. I hope the other parties realize that and stand up against it. They can do it. It requires some courage."

blocks.caption: The nonagenarian, seen here with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is still active in Germany's public lifeImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At almost 94 years old, Knobloch is one of the most prominent and well-known representatives of Jewish life in Germany and one of the last surviving witnesses of Nazi dictatorship between 1933 and 1945. Born in 1932, she was initially raised by her grandmother, who was deported to the Theresienstadt concentration camp in 1942 and died there. A family acquaintance saved the girl by accommodating her on her farm in Middle Franconia and passing her off as her own child.
'Danger looming'
Knobloch said she still thinks about that horrible era every day.

"There were times when this happened only rarely. When it was mentioned by the media from time to time, but not permanently. These days, I wake up thinking about it, and I also go to bed thinking about it," she said.

blocks.caption: Knobloch spoke to DW correspondent Tina Gerhäusser in MunichImage: DW

blocks.text: Knobloch served as vice president of the World Jewish Congress from 2005 to 2013, and as president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany from 2006 to 2010. She has been warning against growing antisemitism in Germany for years, but even she did not foresee the rise of far-right extremist parties like the AfD.
"There's a danger looming that did not exist in this form 10 years ago," she said. "There have always been Nazis, there have always been Jew haters, but not in the way as it's the case today."

In Knobloch's view, the established parties have up to now failed to speak out decisively against the AfD. "Today's political parties must jointly, not alone, address the issue," she said. "I still see a chance here, that people will at least be willing to listen and discuss it. And that's very, very important."
Young people need to be included in the conversation
Knobloch said politicians have to speak more intensively with people and address their fears, especially with young people, adding that this isn't happening enough.

"There's talk about it, but there is no real discussion, because young people are naturally afraid that what they say will become public. What I want to say is, we'll have to find ways to bring young people back into the fold," she said.

After speaking out against the AfD in the wake of the election, Knobloch was targeted with death threats. On Thursday, a witness discovered the scrawled threats on a park bench and a rubbish bin in the English Garden in Munich and informed the police, according to a police headquarters statement. Knobloch subsequently canceled her attendance at an event. The threats were directly linked to the AfD's election victory in Saxony-Anhalt, a spokeswoman said in response to a query from the dpa news agency.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Why do authoritarian regimes target the LGBTQ+ community?
articles.summary: A recent crackdown on the LGBTQ+ community in Turkey is symptomatic of a wider rights regression, according to experts. It's worse under authoritarian regimes, but why is it such a popular policy for…

image.caption: Members of the Turkish LGBTQ+ community were targeted by authorities, and they are not alone (file photo from June 27, 2026)Image: Murat Kocabas/Middle East Images/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Raids on gay bars and homes, hundreds of arrests and rhetoric about state responsibility to "protect families and children." Turkey's latest crackdown on LGBTQ+ communities is not such an outlier.
"It's not uncommon, we've seen it before," Dr Koen Slootmaeckers, from the international politics department at City St George's, University of London, told DW.

"Turkey's been doing this for a while, but it seems like a much higher intensity," Slootmaeckers said. "We've seen it in different places too. I think what we are seeing with the rise of the far right is a crackdown on anything that looks different. It's really about an us versus them narrative and a reinforcing of 'traditional family values.'"

Those values were cited by Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek after the weekend's crackdown: "As per the duty to protect families and children given to the state by the constitution, no criminal organization, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated!"
Attack on LGBTQ+ rights accelerating

The reference to protecting children from harm is also typical of authoritarian government actions against LGBTQ+ communities on a wider scale, added Slootmaeckers, whose work often focuses on gender and sexuality policy.
Slovakia debates marriage equality
"They're trying to bring back discourses around paedophilia and homosexuality being intertwined. It's not always direct but there is a definite tendency."
Sentiments such as those expressed by Gurlek have become increasingly normalized of late, according to a 2026 report from South Africa-based civil rights nonprofit, Civicus.
"Women's and LGBTQI+ people's rights are under the most coordinated and wide-ranging attack in decades," the report reads.

It adds that "The USA has set the global narrative" under President Donald Trump and points to the recent criminalizing of same sex relationships in Burkina Faso and Trinidad and Tobago among its evidence of rights regressions.
While the methods of oppression vary, Slootmaeckers said the underlying reasons are often, at least partly, opportunistic rather than ideological.
Scapegoating a common strategy

"In authoritarian regimes, as we've seen in Hungary and Poland in the past, there is often a tendency when political power becomes threatened to use these issues as an easy way to scapegoat and distract — by claiming that LGBT people are a threat to the social fabric because they challenge family and the future of the nation, so to speak. It's an easy way of creating a scapegoat and often distracting from other crises," he said.

Turkey was ranked 47 of 49 countries in the annual Rainbow Map compiled by the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association. Countries ranking lower means laws and polcies there aren't LGBTQ+ friendly.
But, for many observers it is countries that are dropping in such rankings that are troubling. One of those is Serbia. It has gradually slipped to 29th spot, below the European average.

Groups associated with President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, have been linked to a wave of violence against an LGBTQ+ community which feels increasingly marginalized. A recent survey from the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights found that 80% of respondents said they avoided holding the hand of their partner in public, for example.
EU hopes put up 'guardrails' amid violence in Serbia
While Serbia is not one of the 64 countries around the world which have laws that criminalize homosexuality, some of which carry the death penalty, there is a definite sense of unease.

"In the Balkans, most countries still want to join the EU, so there ar some kind of guardrails on how far they can go. But we see things like [Vucic] trying to cancel [pan-European LGBTQ+ event] EuroPride in 2022 in Belgrade when he felt threatened surrounding Kosovo," said Slootmaeckers, who wrote a book called "Coming in: Sexual politics and EU accession in Serbia" in 2025.
Will Hungary's new govt. bring real change on LGBTQ+ rights?

"We can see this tactic of pandering to family values and then positioning LGBT rights as an expensive frivolity, as a means of redirecting the attention of people from the actual political problem," Slootmaeckers said.

"I think across Europe, not just in the Balkans or Eastern Europe, we see the return of homophobia and transphobia. We see a culture where anything considered 'out there' is threatened and it becomes normalized that we can exclude people again."

Exclusion appears to be the word for many in the Turkish LGBTQ+ community, with rights group Kaos GL, whose offices were raided, calling the latest crackdown "state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society."
For those living under authoritarian regimes elsewhere, the threat of similar scenes continues to loom.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran says it was 'not my decision' to drop Macklemore from tour
articles.summary: The star says tour promoters took the decision, after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian statements on stage.

blocks.text: Ed Sheeran has posted a long statement on Instagram, saying it was not his decision to drop Macklemore from his current US tour.
The US rapper - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - was ejected from the line-up after making pro-Palestinian statements at two dates in New Jersey.
His comments drew criticism from Jewish groups, after which some venues put pressure on the tour promoters to have him removed from the line-up.

In his statement, external, Sheeran said he had spoken with the venues "at length all week to try and build a bridge" - but the promoters, Messina Touring Group, had ultimately decided to remove Macklemore from the bill.
"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," he wrote. "Macklemore's contract for the tour was with the promoter, not me.
"I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."
The star also attempted to explain his decision not to become embroiled in political issues.

"I am not complicit," he wrote. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care.
"Nor does it mean I don't support causes in my own, personal way."
He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds.
"Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes.
"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: Peace.

"I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed. If we only focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change."
The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which is dedicated to pro-Palestinian protestors at Columbia University and condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.
Some of the audience cheered - but there was almost immediate criticism online.

The Israeli American Council launched a petition demanding his removal from the tour; while the campaign group StopAntisemitism said the musician had ambushed fans with propaganda - a claim that was amplified by the pop star Pink, who reposted it on Instagram.
The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.
Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.
During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
After days of press coverage, Macklemore announced on Monday that he had been dropped from the line-up.
In a statement on Instagram, he said the boycott had been organised by Robert Kraft - the billionaire owner of the Gilette Stadium in Massachusetts.

Kraft - who once hired Ed Sheeran to play at his wedding - confirmed he'd made the decision to bar Macklemore, saying his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric".

"I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.
However, he did not address the claim that he'd asked other venues to put pressure on the tour.

Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."
In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran had been put in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance.

"Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.

He also emphasised that, although he was only able to complete two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."

articles.title: Indonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in Borneo
articles.summary: Critically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blaze

blocks.text: Wildfires in Indonesia are sweeping through a critical research site for Bornean orangutans and are now threatening a celebrated research camp, home to one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild apes.

In the past few days, the fires have burned within 200 metres of Rangkong research station, a satellite of Cabang Panti research station, which lies about four miles north in Gunung Palung national park.

Hundreds of Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species, live in the direct vicinity of the research stations, with more than 2,500 thought to inhabit the park, many areas of which are now on fire. All three orangutan species are considered critically endangered.

“Orangutans are fleeing from these forests. It’s just horrible,” said Prof Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has been leading scientific research on orangutans at Cabang Panti for 32 years.

In most cases, the fires were intentionally set to clear land, as is done every year on the island. But an extremely strong El Niño – a warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean that disrupts global weather patterns – has fuelled exceptionally hot and dry conditions across the country, with fires easily escaping control as a result. In West Kalimantan province, some areas have gone months with little to no rainfall.

blocks.caption: Field assistants fight fires near the Rangkong research station. Photograph: Jessica Laman

blocks.text: Scientists at Cabang Panti have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and their life histories, following some of the same individuals from birth to grandmotherhood. Research carried out at the site has helped to establish the orangutan reproduction cycle, finding that the apes only give birth once every eight years – the longest cycle of any mammal. “The long-term nature of this database and the detailed nature of the database is unparalleled,” Knott said.

But the fires threaten to undo such continuous observations. At the rate the flames are moving, without intervention or large firebreaks, the fires will reach Cabang Panti in 20 days’ time, scientists said.

“[Cabang Panti] protects what has been, until now, one of the only truly ecologically intact tracts of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo,” said Prof Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who ran an orangutan research project at the site from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuously collected field data, we cannot understand how tropical ecosystems are adapting to or suffering from global climate shifts.”

In a desperate effort to save Rangkong research station, a team of more than 40 people – mostly field assistants, staff and local villagers – are fighting day and night to stave off the encroaching inferno. Recently, they constructed a firebreak and an improvised sprinkler system using a punctured hose line around the station to saturate the surrounding peat.

blocks.caption: Burnt forest near Palangka Raya, in Central Kalimantan province this week. Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/Reuters

blocks.text: Once fire reaches a peat swamp, it can smoulder underground for months – even after surface flames have been extinguished. Keeping the peat wet is therefore a key defence.

“The issue has surpassed any local organisation’s capacity,” said Caitlin O’Connell, deputy director of the Gunung Palung orangutan conservation programme. “We need large-scale water bombing and skilled firefighters.”
Even if they manage to save the research station, it may be for nothing if the orangutans lose their home.

“The orangutans need the forest,” Knott said. “If all we have left is the building, what are we studying if the orangutans are all gone, and the food they have is all gone? They can’t survive without that forest.”
As solitary animals, orangutans require large ranges and live at low population densities. “You can’t just shove them all together in what remains of the forest,” Knott said.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers prepare to transport a mother and baby orangutan named Raya and Rayu who were rescued from wildfires in East Kotawaringin, Central Kalimantan province. Photograph: Reina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Those leading the on-the-ground fire response have already witnessed the impact on the apes. “Five orangutans from our long-term study population were observed fleeing the fire, some only metres from the flames,” said Wahyu Susanto, research director for Yayasan Palung, an Indonesian NGO that protects Bornean orangutans. “These are individuals that we have followed and studied for years.”
Indonesian meteorologists predict an intense fire season persisting through October as climate forecasts point to a strengthening El Niño.

“The hotspots are everywhere,” O’Connell said. “I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say that what we thought couldn’t burn could actually completely disappear if we’re looking at these dry conditions going on for months.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: Iran war has led to US munitions shortfalls, Pentagon inspector confirms
articles.summary: The inspector also found a bottleneck in resupply, despite President Donald Trump's claims that US supplies are "virtually limitless".

blocks.text: The US defence department's inspector general says the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump who has repeatly denied the US is facing shortages.
Trump has claimed US munitions supplies are "virtually unlimited" and said reporting otherwise is "fake news".
But the independent watchdog said the US spent more than $22 billion on munitions from February through June, leading to "strategic inventory shortfalls".
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment about the discrepancy.
The new report provides a first-of-its-kind, independent glimpse into US weapons stockpiles, data that is typically classified.
Previous estimates have painted a dire picture of the US shortages.
Over the course of the war, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept incoming Iranian attacks.

A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, found that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half.
The inspector general's report did not disclose exactly how many of the weapons remain.
It did, however, note the inventory shortfalls and reveal "industrial base bottlenecks" for munitions resupply.
The report added that the defence department is now working to "streamline procurement processes and production lead times" to address the shortages and "respond rapidly to a contingency".
Trump and other administration officials have sought to cast reports of shortages as false and "treasonous".
In a 4 August X post, for example, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth described news reporting on the shortages as "not true".
And in a lengthy Truth Social post on 3 September, Trump claimed that the US had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition and is "stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen".
The watchdog's report also notes that equipment losses have totaled $3.7bn, with other $7.4bn in other expenditures. Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war from 28 Feb to 30 Jun.
Among the losses have been four F-15e fighter jets, a highly advanced F-35 Joint Strike Fighter and 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed in "various circumstances".
When US and Israeli strikes began, Trump repeatedly said that the conflict would be over within weeks.
More recently, he said the conflict might not end until "right after" the November midterm elections in the US.
Polls show that the war is unpopular among Americans.

One Reuters/Ipsos poll released in early September found that only 23% of Americans - and only half of Republicans - believe the US to be in a stronger position with Iran compared with before hostilities broke out.

articles.title: Alexander Ovechkin backs Putin party in campaign video
articles.summary: Ice hockey legend Alexander Ovechkin has lent Vladimir Putin's party a helping hand in its parliamentary election campaign. That's in keeping with a pattern of support by an athlete who claims not to…

image.caption: Alexander Ovechkin is set to play his 22nd season in the NHLImage: IMAGO/ITAR-TASS

blocks.text: When Russia's parliamentary elections are held from September 18 to 20, Alexander Ovechkin won't be there to cast his ballot in person. On Monday he took his first few strides back on the ice in the United States as he starts gearing up for a new National Hockey League (NHL) season with the Washington Capitals, his 22nd in the world's best league.

Before leaving his homeland, where he spent his summer break, he did make his contribution to the election campaign, however, appearing in a video promoting the ruling United Russia party, which steadfastly supports President Vladimir Putin.

In the video, which has been widely shared on social media, Ovechkin doesn't speak but can be clearly seen in the third row of a group of supporters behind Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who is heading the United Russia list for the parliamentary vote.

Ovechkin's appearance has faced criticism, including from Ukrainian skeleton pilot Vladyslav Heraskevych, who was disqualified from the 2026 Olympic Games for insisting on wearing a helmet depicting athletes killed in Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ovechkin a long-standing Putin supporter
This is certainly not the first time that Ovechkin has expressed his support for Putin, with whom he shares his profile photo on his Instagram account.

blocks.caption: Ovechkin's Instagram account features a profile photo of him with PutinImage: @aleksandrovechkinofficial/instagram

blocks.text: And, at times, Ovechkin's public support has appeared even more active than in the current United Russia video. Back in 2017, Ovechkin used his Instagram account to announce the creation of "PutinTeam" a group to help support Putin in the 2018 presidential campaign.

"I have never hidden my feelings about our president; I have always openly supported him. I am certain there are many of us who support Vladimir Putin! So let's unite and show the world a strong, united Russia!" he wrote.
"Being part of such a team is a source of pride for me; it feels just like pulling on the Russian national team jersey, knowing the whole country is rooting for you."

The creation of PutinTeam came three years after Russia had invaded and seized the Ukrainian territory Crimea in 2014, a move that was met with widespread condemnation in the international community. Later that year, Ovechkin appeared to express support for the operation, posting a photo of himself on Instagram holding up a sign with the message: "#savechildrenfromfascism."
"Our grandfathers and grandmothers witnessed all the horrors of fascism! We will not let it happen in our time," he wrote.

Putin has painted the Ukrainian authorities as "neo-Nazi" or fascist, in particular when justifying Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022. What Putin calls a "special military operation" raised questions in the minds of many about how this might affect Ovechkin's view of the man he had always so publicly supported.
On February 25, 2022, a day after Russia launched the invasion, a reporter covering the Washington Capitals asked Ovechkin if he still supported Putin.
"Well, he's my president," Ovechkin replied. "But how I said, I'm not in politics, I'm an athlete."
He did issue a vague appeal for peace but declined to criticize Moscow's military action.
"Please, no more war. It doesn't matter who's in the war — Russia, Ukraine, different countries," he said.
Capitals: 'Ovechkin asked by his country'
Approached for comment on Tuesday, the NHL referred reporters to the Washington Capitals.
"Alex Ovechkin is a Russian citizen who ‌lives in Moscow with his family during the offseason and will ‌live ​there following his retirement," team spokesperson Sergey Kocharov said in the statement.

"This summer, while in Russia, he was asked by his country to participate in a ​video campaign. As the longest-tenured athlete in Washington, D.C., and a pillar of the community, his focus and ours is on the season ahead and the ⁠continued impact ​he makes on the ice and in our ​city."
Back on the ice
Whatever you may think of his political views, Ovechkin is without a doubt one of the best players to ever lace on a pair of skates.

Now, back on the ice in Arlington, Virginia, ahead of the Washington Capitals' training camp, "Great8" is focused on getting his aging body (he turns 41 on Thursday) ready to compete for what would be a second Stanley Cup for both him and the Caps.

For much of the offseason, Ovechkin had left open whether he would return for another year. After all, he has achieved just about everything you can in the NHL, having broken Wayne Gretzky's career goal-scoring record two seasons ago. Going into the 2025-26 campaign he has 929 goals in 1,573 regular season games. In July though, after a conversation with his wife, he decided to come back for one more year in Washington – and he hasn't ruled out extending his career beyond that.
Over 40 and still going strong

"I'm going to be 41. I've had a lot of pressure on my shoulders over the years," he said. "I'm going to focus on the game and helping my team to win," he told reporters after his first skate. "I'm still a good player and can still help the team to win."
His numbers support that last assertion, having scored 32 goals in 2025-26. Only two other players have ever scored more over the age of 40.
"I can't wait for the season," he said. "On paper, you can see our team is one of the best teams but now we have to work for the Stanley Cup."
The bookies disagree, however, with some putting the Capitals way down at 18 (of 32) on their list of Stanley Cup candidates for 2027.
On the other hand, the prospect of United Russia's winning this weekend's parliamentary elections, the first since the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, appears a safe bet.

articles.title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
articles.summary: The announcement by the US points to a developing field of modern warfare in the Earth's orbit.

blocks.text: The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena.

Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.
So what could this weapon be, and what is wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry?

Advanced militaries already deploy satellites in space for range of purposes, from supplying secure communications to reconnaissance, and providing precise location information for targeted strikes and detecting missile launches.
As warfare become more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase.

Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US.
"I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless."
Bowen also would not rule out some sort of more disruptive and riskier weaponry, which could create a lot of debris and destruction.
"Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said.
"Possibly some sort of close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well."
But while the weapon placed in orbit appears to be a first, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time.
In fact in the last 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites.

"Theoretically, these RPO sats can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC.
Bowen adds that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit."
This, he says, can be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites.
Thornton says that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability.

"The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike sats in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he says.

"From the Russian point of view they see Nato as having much better and more sats than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat."
Thornton adds a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EPM blast would 'fry' any unhardened sats over a wide expanse."

He says that, having so few satellites, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, which would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring sats designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers".

articles.title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial oil pipeline
articles.summary: Experts tell BBC Verify the pipeline's closure could cut oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day.

blocks.text: Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher.

The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war.

The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen.
New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week.
The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks.

It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping.

articles.title: Canada is a 'safe harbour' for global finance, Carney says
articles.summary: The prime minister is hosting a major global investment summit, with the goal of attracting investment amid a trade war with the US.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney has pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" for some of the world's largest investors to spend their money in an era of geopolitical and economic uncertainty.

The country is "perfectly situated to build in the new global economic order", he told more than 100 global investors and sovereign wealth fund representatives gathered in Toronto for a major investment summit.
The group represent more than C$120tn ($86tn; £64tn) of assets. Carney's ambition is that they will invest in sectors like defence, energy, mining, AI and infrastructure.
Ottawa hopes they can be sold on more than 160 projects, from data centres to pipelines, and help Canada weather its trade war with the US.

Canada's dispute with its largest trade partner has prompted Carney to look to expand economic partnerships with Europe, Asia and the Middle East as he seeks to reduce his country's reliance on its neighbour to the south.
"Our goal is simple: to make Canada the most attractive place in the G7 to invest," Carney said on Tuesday morning.

As part of that move, Carney announced plans to privatise operations for four of the country's largest airports, saying it would raise billions of dollars that could be reinvested in transport infrastructure.

Many of the business leaders attending the event in Toronto received a personal invitation from the prime minister, who worked in the top tiers of global finance and was a central banker before turning to politics.
Much of the action will take place in private sessions and bilateral meetings over the course of the day.
There will, however, be panels with speakers including Deutsche Bank AG CEO Christian Sewing, Bombardier executive Eric Martel, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.
For Carney, the event will be a test of whether he can deliver on his promise to strengthen the country's economic resilience.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month and the two countries have since imposed tit-for-tat tariffs.
On Tuesday, new US tariffs came into effect on a number of Canadian goods while some others were lifted, and bans on goods like alcohol and motorcycles are due to come into force next week.
On Tuesday, Carney addressed the American executives in Toronto directly.
"To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas," he said.
"After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties."

Meanwhile, protestors on Monday accused the Carney government of organising a "great Canadian sell-off" of public resources and infrastructure to corporate interests, and hundreds appeared outside the opening night gala at a downtown museum.
"Half the buyers that he has invited here to Toronto are American," said Kai Nagata, with advocacy group Dogwood, on Monday.
"Let's be clear, every piece of our country that we sell off to American billionaires brings us closer to becoming the 51st state."

articles.title: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, Oman says
articles.summary: Iran says El Gaia caught fire after hitting mines, but the US says the oil tanker was struck by a missile and then a drone.

blocks.text: Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman says.

Oman's Maritime Security Centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room, adding that the vessel was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula.
On Monday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route.
But the US military insisted the Iranian report was false. It said the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre, meanwhile, said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel that was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday.
Earlier this month, Iran made a similar claim about an incident that killed two Filipino sailors on a Saudi-owned oil supertanker in the crucial waterway.

The Revolutionary Guards said the vessel, Sidr, caught fire after hitting a naval mine. But Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran and maritime security firms reported that it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam.

The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

articles.title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father
articles.summary:
Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir

The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad

blocks.text: The sons of Imran Khan have accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions.

Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges.
They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK to Pakistan to lobby for his release.

On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft.

blocks.caption: Imran Khan outside court in Lahore after a hearing in February 2023. Photograph: Mohsin Raza/Reuters

blocks.text: Later this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release.

Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”.

“The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.”

blocks.caption: Left to right: Sulaiman Khan, Jemima Khan, Imran Khan’s daughter Tyrian White and Kasim Khan at a film premiere in London in February 2023. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

blocks.text: Late last month, Sky Sports aired an interview with Khasim and Sulaiman during its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister, made a formal complaint to Sky Sports after the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break.

“It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.”

The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.
Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said.
Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief.

blocks.caption: Asim Munir praying after laying a wreath on the martyrs’ monument during a ceremony in Rawalpindi last year. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: When Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and the bad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2023, the persecution of Khan increased notably.

“It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman. Munir’s powers expanded over the past year as he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”.

Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention.
Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party.

“There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off.
“The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.”

In a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.
“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said.

It was widely acknowledged that Khan came to power in 2018 with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption, press censorship and persecution of his opponents.
He was toppled in 2022 after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government.

By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor to the persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power.
Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf display a poster of Imran Khan at a rally in February on the second anniversary of the 2024 general elections, which the party alleges were rigged. Photograph: Bilawal Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Sulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case.
Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying.
They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence.

“We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.”

Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.”

Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”

articles.title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
articles.summary: The Danish prime minister has accused Russia of "reckless" behaviour, while the Kremlin is yet to comment.

blocks.text: Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its helicopters while it was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea.
The Danish government has summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said happened during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide".
Moscow has not commented on the incident.

It came on the same day Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania in the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In a statement detailing the incident in the Baltic Sea, the Danish armed forces said: "One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser."
Of the two flares fired at the helicopter, one passed close to it, the statement added.
The Danish foreign ministry described the incident as "completely unacceptable".
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen accused Russia of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour", adding: "That is something we cannot accept."
Overnight, Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace.
Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.
The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said, but the country's president pointed to increased Russian aggression in recent months.

President Gitanas Nausėda wrote on X: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our Nato Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."
Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".
It said the overnight operations were of a "preventive nature" and aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions".
Nato jets have been scrambled several times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.
Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
articles.summary: Trains were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday after objects were found on tracks at multiple locations.

blocks.text: Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway operator has said.
ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while several level crossings were also malfunctioning.
Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action".
It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating. The BBC has contacted police for comment.
The network's website showed that 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected.
ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved".

Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands.

articles.title: What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer?
articles.summary:
After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral

Recently, I may have…

blocks.text: Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.

On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.

Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.

I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.

As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.

The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.

Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.

blocks.caption: The problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking, believe some experts. Photograph: DB Pictures/Alamy

blocks.text: So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.

For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.

Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.

In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.

“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”

blocks.caption: People vacate buildings marked for demolition in Satya Niketan after the collapse of a five-storey building. Photograph: Vishal Kapoor/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.

India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.

For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.

In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.

A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)

“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.

Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Xi Jinping, far right, with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and India’s Narendra Modi at this year’s Brics summit. Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/EPA

blocks.text: New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.

Political donations | An investigation by the BBC’s Shubhangi Misra claimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.

Women’s health support | Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introduce a women’s health programme that will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assess the physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.
after newsletter promotion

Calling all emerging writers | Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Poet Parag Pawan’s book.

blocks.text: This week, write and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:

“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.

A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Umar Khalid, who has spent six years in an Indian jail without trial.

blocks.text: That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check

blocks.caption: World’s fastest paper delivery service? Ayan Shaikh at work in Ahmedabad. Photograph: Instagram

blocks.text: As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.

Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.

“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.
